abstract: |
  Conservation decisions under deep uncertainty require models that produce plausible ecosystem projections at a tractable computational cost. Sensitivity-guided model development and ensemble calibration are established in other fields, but remain uncommon in marine ecological projections. A workflow that uses distribution-based sensitivity analysis of Great Barrier Reef coral demographic data to guide model structure is presented here. Colony size was the dominant factor associated with growth and among the leading factors associated with survival; functional group and location-specific conditions also contributed. These findings informed Kora, a size-structured population model that tracks five coral functional groups using growth and background-survival relationships fitted to observations. Kora also represents heat-stress mortality, thermal-tolerance inheritance, reproduction, and recruitment. Ensemble calibration at two reefs reproduced observed coral-cover trajectories despite contrasting monitoring histories. The workflow provides a practical basis for uncertainty-aware projections where monitoring is sparse and rapid exploration of management scenarios is needed.

# Introduction

Coral reef ecosystems face rapid global decline driven by climate change, with mass
bleaching events increasing in both frequency and severity [@bozecRapidlyClosingWindow2025;
@hughesGlobalWarmingTransforms2018; @eakinSevereWidespreadCoral2026]. Conservation decisions
must be made today despite profound uncertainty about future conditions and system response,
with consequences unfolding over decades. This condition of deep uncertainty, in which
probability distributions over key drivers cannot be reliably specified
[@lempertUseDecisionMaking2024], motivates decision support tools capable of exploring a
wide range of plausible futures rather than optimizing against a single projected outcome.
Computational tractability of models underpinning decision support is therefore a core
design requirement: the model must be able to evaluate thousands of scenarios at low cost to
inform timely development of effective policies [cf. @arnoldAdhocModellingStrategic2020].

A persistent challenge is determining the appropriate model structure for a given purpose.
The model must capture the relevant dynamics, be defensibly parameterized, and make its
assumptions explicit so users can judge the credibility and limits of its projections
[@jakemanNormalizingGoodPractice2024; @liResponseCommentWhen2026]. It must also be
sufficiently computationally efficient to evaluate large scenario ensembles to provide
timely insights under deep uncertainty [cf. @lempertUseDecisionMaking2024;
@stantonDecisionMakingDeep2021; @lamontagneLargeEnsembleAnalytic2018]. Marine ecosystems
compound this challenge as direct observation is costly, continuous monitoring is typically
infeasible, and data sparsity means expert knowledge heavily shapes model design, risking
the introduction of factors whose influence is negligible [@bodeRevealingBeliefsUsing2017]
or the use of data that is not representative of the system being modeled
[@wengerAssessingTransferabilityEcological2012; @sergeEvaluationAllenCoral2024].

Here we outline a workflow for model development on coral demographics using data from the
EcoRRAP monitoring program [Ecological Intelligence for Reef Restoration and Adaptation
Program, @australianinstituteofmarinescienceEcologicalIntelligenceReef2025], which has
generated colony-level observations via orthorectified photomosaics across reefs in
Australia's Great Barrier Reef (GBR) and the Torres Strait
[@australianinstituteofmarinescienceaimsEcoRRAPCoralDemographic2023]. The photomosaic
derived data was complemented by in situ measurements for corals under 5cm diameter and
across all sites [@doropoulosImpactEnvironmentalGradients2025]. A moment-independent global
sensitivity analysis method [@pianosiSimpleEfficientMethod2015;
@pianosiDistributionbasedSensitivityAnalysis2018] is applied to data from the Offshore North
and Torres Strait regions, as well as two specific reefs (Moore Reef and Masig Reef) to
discern key factors that drive estimates of annualized growth and survival across five
dominant functional groups of hard coral, including tabular *Acropora*, corymbose
*Acropora*, branching non-*Acropora*, small massive (and encrusting) taxa, and large massive
taxa. Definition of these functional groups are informed by prior work
[@bozecRapidlyClosingWindow2025].

Ecological knowledge identifies many plausible influences on coral growth and survival but
available data cannot resolve them all. We therefore use sensitivity analysis of observed
demographic variation to guide the structure of the fitted demographic models at the spatial
scales studied. Factors whose influence cannot be distinguished from a random-noise
benchmark are not included as explicit predictors. This limits model complexity by excluding
data that are not reliably influential for the purpose at hand. Sensitivity-guided model
development is established in hydrology
[@vanwerkhovenSensitivityguidedReductionParametric2009] and terrestrial ecosystem modeling
[@neilCalibratingMulticonstraintEnsemble2025; @wangGlobalSensitivityAnalyses2025], but
remains uncommon in marine ecological projections.

In watershed models, sensitivity-guided screening has reduced the number of parameters
requiring calibration [@vanwerkhovenSensitivityguidedReductionParametric2009]; in crop
models, it has improved prediction quality [@wangGlobalSensitivityAnalyses2025]. More
broadly, sensitivity analysis can help assess whether added model complexity is warranted
[@douglas-smithCertainTrendsUncertainty2020; @pianosiSensitivityAnalysisEnvironmental2016a].
For coral reefs, this approach may be particularly useful where monitoring is limited and
the influence of environmental conditions varies between sites. No single environmental
variable, for example, consistently predicted the survival of seeded corals across three GBR
reefs [@jurriaansWaveEnergyOther2025]. Assessing observed growth and survival at the spatial
scale of interest can therefore help determine which factors the available data support as
explicit predictors, and where and what further monitoring might help resolve. Factors that
cannot be resolved from available data should not be assumed ecologically unimportant; nor
should relationships identified at one location be assumed to transfer to another
[@wengerAssessingTransferabilityEcological2012].

The sensitivity analysis informed Kora's design as a size-structured population model with
annual timesteps. Growth and mortality functions are parameterized
separately per functional group via polynomial regression on field observations. Sub-second
simulation performance enables the extensive ensemble exploration that model-informed
decision support requires, as well as enabling rapid hypothesis testing, iterative model
refinement, and use in direct stakeholder engagement settings.

The current implementation of Kora operates on a single representative reef area. The
model's ability to plausibly reproduce observed historic coral cover trajectories is
demonstrated and assessed at two reefs chosen to span the range of monitoring effort typical
of GBR management. These are Moore Reef, with several decades of LTMP manta-tow records
which provide estimates of total coral cover across large transects, and Masig Reef, where
only a few years of photogrammetry-derived cover estimates are available.

Ecological realism is established through ensemble calibration with estimates of coral cover
around the reef perimeter (manta-tow observations) collected by the AIMS LTMP (Long-Term
Monitoring Program). Parametric uncertainty and identifiability were then explicitly
quantified. That the same workflow calibrates successfully from either data source indicates
applicability extends to reefs where historic monitoring is limited or absent; a typical
condition across many of the world's coral reefs.

# Model development workflow {#sec-model-development-workflow}

The overarching aim of the model is to provide indicative projections of coral demographic
dynamics under ambient and disturbed conditions (principally marine heatwaves). Parsimony is
achieved by identifying factors that represent the dynamics of dominant coral functional
groups and their respective contributions to overall coral cover, as evidenced by available
data. To this end, empirical sensitivity analysis was conducted on EcoRRAP data
[@australianinstituteofmarinescienceaimsEcoRRAPCoralDemographic2023] and associated
environmental observations to identify principal drivers of growth and survival dynamics.
Nine factors are assessed (@tbl-1).

the range is taken over all observations. The `functional_group` count is the number of
groups, not the number of taxon–functional-group assignments; genus-level *Acropora* records
contribute to both *Acropora* groups. For all other factors, the count is the number of

is also given. @stbl-12 lists the survey-code mappings used for the assignments reported
below. N/A indicates a factor was not available for that region. {#tbl-1}

The sensitivity analysis informed model structure, reducing equifinality and parameter
identifiability concerns. Equifinality refers to the case in which multiple parameter
combinations produce similar, equally plausible outcomes. Identifiability is the ability to
attribute cause and effect to any single parameter or a unique parameter set
[@guillaumeIntroductoryOverviewIdentifiability2019;
@luoParameterIdentifiabilityConstraint2009]. In high-dimensional cases (e.g., models with
many parameters), factors can interact, with parameter combinations effectively compensating
for one another, making it difficult to determine which factors genuinely influence modeled
outcomes. Factor interaction and compensation degrade both model interpretability and
predictive reliability, hence the common advice to retain as much simplicity as possible
consistent with the model's purpose [@jakemanTenIterativeSteps2006;
@majonePitfallsAnalysis1980]. Representing all possible influences on coral growth and
mortality would substantially increase model dimensionality, leading to identifiability
issues and inflated computational cost inconsistent with the goal of supporting timely
model-informed decision-making.

The EcoRRAP monitoring program has collected colony-level demographic observations across
the study area (GBR and Torres Strait) via orthorectified photomosaics since 2021
[@gordonFieldPhotogrammetry4D2023; @gordonFieldPhotogrammetry4D2025;
@toorFieldPhotogrammetry4D2025]. Each photomosaic campaign produces spatially and temporally
registered imagery from which individual coral colonies are digitized [precision 1.6mm,
@lecheneEvaluatingErrorSources2024], colony diameters estimated from their digitized areas
assuming circular geometry and survival status at successive timepoints. These data were
complemented with *in situ* data for juvenile coral demographics
[@doropoulosImpactEnvironmentalGradients2025], collected from within the same plots.

To demonstrate Kora in settings with different monitoring histories and coral community
compositions, we selected two reefs for model calibration and evaluation. Moore Reef has a
long monitoring record that enables calibration against historical cover dynamics. Masig
Reef has a shorter record and a different community composition, providing a data-limited
contrast. Their locations are shown in @fig-1.

We assessed the influence of environmental and ecological factors on growth and survival
using observations from the broader regions containing these reefs: the GBR Offshore North
for Moore Reef and the Torres Strait for Masig Reef. We counted each taxonomic category once
per assigned functional group, consolidating survey codes to genus where possible and
retaining family-level labels as separate categories; genus-level *Acropora* was counted in
both assigned groups. For the GBR Offshore North, data from Moore
and Lizard Reefs were collected over February 2021 to October 2023, spanning up to 17
taxon–functional-group assignments (16 for growth, 17 for survival). This comprised 6,772
growth observations and 10,652 survival observations across 43 plots inclusive of two depth
strata (shallow and deep), grouped into 7 monitoring sites, with mean survey intervals of
321 days for growth
observations (SD: 86 days) and 329 days for survival observations (SD: 75 days); range
118–488 days for both.

For the Torres Strait, data from Aukane, Dungeness, and Masig Reefs were collected over
April 2021 to March 2023, spanning 15 taxon–functional-group assignments for both growth
and survival. The observations comprised 3,524 growth observations and 5,839 survival
observations across 51 plots, grouped into 10 monitoring sites, with a mean survey interval
of 336 days (SD: 6 days; range: 323–357 days). For both regions, the observations span four
habitat types (reef
back, flank, front, and lagoon). Interested readers are directed to the relevant Standard
Operating Procedures for further details on data collection
[@gordonFieldPhotogrammetry4D2023], photomosaic production
[@gordonFieldPhotogrammetry4D2025], and coral-colony digitization
[@toorFieldPhotogrammetry4D2025].

![Panel A: Map of Australia's Great Barrier Reef with the study reefs marked; other reef
outlines in gray. Panel B: Close up of the Torres Strait study reefs (Masig Reef marked with
an orange star). Panel C: Close up of the Offshore North region and study reefs (Moore Reef
marked with a blue star). Stars indicate the reefs selected for model calibration and

Raw transitions between successive observations were standardized to annual rates via Euler
approximation (see @sec-growth-models), accounting for the variable interval between
surveys. Of the nine factors assessed, two (longitude and latitude; see @tbl-1) describe the
spatial location of monitoring activities rather than an environmental condition, but were
retained for completeness.

Demographic observations were combined with observed depth measurements at each monitored
site. Modeled wave-induced bottom current speed (at 10m resolution) was included for the
Offshore North region only [@callaghanGreatBarrierReef2023;
@callaghanWaveModellingProxy2015]. Daily sea water temperature estimates, available for both
regions, were obtained from the eReefs GBR1 Hydro v2 hydrodynamic model [\~1km resolution,
monthly time step, at multiple depth levels ranging from 2.35 m to 18 m,
@bairdCSIROEnvironmentalModelling2020; @stevenEReefsOperationalInformation2019] via the
*eReefs* portal (extraction ID: 2608.25b1bb7, https://portal.ereefs.org.au/). Where
temperature records at the target depth of 9m were unavailable, records from the nearest
shallower eReefs depth were used (see Supplementary A). These variables were included as
candidate predictors given established evidence that temperature and localized wave energy
influence coral growth and recovery patterns [@pratchettSpatialTemporalTaxonomic2015;
@jurriaansWaveEnergyOther2025; @warneMathematicalModellingUncertainty2025;
@whitmanSeededAcroporaDigitifera2025], and on the basis of recommendations from the
literature [@alvarez-noriegaSpatialVariationUpper2024].

## The PAWN method

PAWN [named after the creators, @pianosiDistributionbasedSensitivityAnalysis2018,
@pianosiSimpleEfficientMethod2015] is a moment-independent method originally developed to
assess sensitivity of model outputs to input factors. It quantifies the individual factor
influence on output distributions by comparing the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of
observations conditioned on specific factor values against the unconditional CDF. The method
captures non-linear relationships, threshold effects and interactions through its
distribution-based comparisons. Conceptual simplicity is a further advantage, aiding
communication of results to stakeholders unfamiliar with sensitivity analysis. The objective
of the sensitivity analysis is to screen for factors that influence observed demographic
patterns (or are sufficient proxies for such dynamics), providing an empirical basis for
structural decisions during model development (@sec-model-development).

Diameter and survival at $t + 1$ were modeled as dependent variables, with diameter at $t$
and other environmental and ecological factors as predictors (overview in @tbl-1). Analyses
were conducted for each functional group (detailed in @sec-functional-groups). To establish
a baseline for factor significance, a random noise variable [a "dummy" factor, cf.
@khorashadizadehComparisonVariancebasedMomentindependent2017] was included in all
analyses, providing an objective threshold. Factors whose influence was indistinguishable
from random variation were considered non-influential and excluded.

Summary statistics across slices produce a single sensitivity index for each factor. Here, a
"slice" is a conditioning interval for a given factor ($x_{i}$), formed by partitioning the
observed range of $x_{i}$ into $N_{s}$ quantile-based intervals, where $N_{s}$ denotes the
number of slices. Within each slice ($I_{k}$, $k \in \lbrack 1,N_{s}\rbrack$), the subset of
output observations corresponding to $x_{i} \in I_{k}$ is used to construct the conditional
CDF ($\Phi_{Y}|x_{i}\left( y \middle| x_{i} \in I_{k} \right)$). A larger $N_{s}$ produces
finer conditioning intervals and a more detailed characterization of the output distribution
but requires proportionally larger samples to avoid sparse slices. The PAWN method is
detailed here as:

$${PAWN_{x_{i}} = stat\left\{ KS\left\lbrack \Phi_{Y} \middle| x_{i}\left( y \middle| x_{i} \in I_{k} \right),\ \Phi_{Y} \right\rbrack \right\}
}$$

$${PAWN_{i} = \frac{PAWN_{x_{i}} - PAWN_{dummy}}{\sigma}}$$ {#eq-pawn}

Where:

- $x_{i}$ is the factor of interest (depth, diameter at time $t$, etc.)

- $\Phi_{Y}|x_{i}\left( y \middle| x_{i} \in I_{k} \right)$ is the conditional CDF of output
  $y$ (growth or survival) when $x_{i}$ is constrained to slice $k$

- $\Phi_{Y}$ is the unconditioned CDF of output $y$ (diameter or survival at $t + 1$)

- $stat$ indicates the summary statistic of interest, such as the mean, median, min/max calculated over a set of randomly sampled values of $x_{i}$

- $KS$ denotes the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test statistic, of which a summary statistic ($stat$)
  is taken across slices

- $PAWN_{x_{i}}$ is the PAWN sensitivity index for factor $x_{i}$

- $PAWN_{dummy}$ is the index for the random noise variable

- $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the raw PAWN indices across all factors and summary
  statistics in a given analysis. As a single scaling constant per analysis, it does not
  change the ordering of factors or their position relative to $PAWN_{dummy}$.

- $PAWN_{i}$ is the reported index for a given summary statistic (mean, median, etc.)

Larger values of $PAWN_{i}$ indicate greater influence relative to the dummy factor,
expressed in units of the standard deviation of raw PAWN indices for that analysis. Negative
values indicate factors whose raw indices fall below the random-noise benchmark, providing a
screening criterion for excluding predictors that the available data do not resolve as
influential. While the median of slices is typically the reported measure, the mean is
adopted here as the primary sensitivity statistic, as it better captures the influence of a
factor across its full range, including regions where its effect is strongest. Here, the
Kolmogorov-Smirnov test statistic is adopted to quantify the maximum difference between
CDFs, although alternate statistical tests can be applied. This process is repeated for all
factors of interest using 10 slices (i.e., $N_{s} ≔ 10$) per factor following
@pianosiDistributionbasedSensitivityAnalysis2018.

## Results of sensitivity analysis {#sec-results-of-sensitivity-analysis}

Colony diameter screened in as an influential factor for predicting growth (i.e., annualized
increase in estimated diameter) and survival in the Offshore North and Torres Strait regions
(@fig-2 A, B; @fig-3 A, B). Additional PAWN analysis across binned diameter classes
indicates that the influence of diameter on growth is greatest at the largest diameters in
both regions, and is also high at the smallest diameters in the Offshore North (@sfig-1).
For survival, the influence of diameter is strongest at the smallest diameters (@sfig-2).
Functional group identity was also a source of variation in predicted growth, though less so
than colony diameter.

In the Offshore North, depth and the temporally aggregated eReefs (mean and max) temperature
also screened above the dummy threshold. The temperature signal partly reflects between-reef
differences: Lizard Island and Moore Reef are separated by roughly 2.2° of latitude
(@tbl-1). A separation large enough to produce distinct baseline thermal regimes between the
two reefs independent of colony-level demographic processes. Binned analysis reveals the
influence of locational differences on survival remain consistent across diameter classes in
the Offshore North (@sfig-2), whereas functional group identity was more prominently
indicated as influential in the Torres Strait. These findings are perhaps to be expected
given the Offshore North is represented by sites across Moore and Lizard Reefs (two large
reefs, with Lizard including granitic islands) with greater variation in environmental
conditions compared to the Torres Strait region (represented by three much smaller reefs
closer in latitude).

At the reef-level, maximum temperature is shown to influence survival at Moore Reef (@fig-3
C), ranking second of the nine factors assessed ($PAWN_{\text{mean}} = 0.843$), ahead of
functional group identity and depth. In comparison, diameter is indicated to play a greater
role towards survival at Masig Reef (@fig-3 D), with functional group identity also
indicated as a secondary influence. Wave-induced bottom current speed ("Bottom Stress") is
not available for the Torres Strait and showed relatively lower sensitivity indices at the
reef level in the Offshore North (ranks 5 and 8 for growth and survival respectively at
Moore Reef). At the regional Offshore North scale, however, bottom stress is indicated as a
more notable factor for survival (rank 4, $PAWN_{\text{mean}} = 0.725$), consistent with
wave exposure varying between Moore and Lizard Reefs. Temperature showed negligible
sensitivity at Masig Reef and for growth across the Offshore North; at Moore Reef its
sensitivity indices indicate a site-level thermal signal for survival (as described above),
while the regional Offshore North survival result additionally incorporates a between-reef
spatial component.

Growth and survival are shown to be largely insensitive to habitat type at reef level for
both regions (@fig-2 C, D and @fig-3 C, D): habitat type falls below the dummy threshold at
Masig Reef and, while marginally above it at Moore Reef, it remains far below colony
diameter and functional group identity. Habitat type remains below the dummy threshold
across nearly all diameter classes at the regional scale, the sole exception being the
smallest Offshore North survival class (@sfig-1 and @sfig-2). One potential interpretation
is that corals observed in monitoring surveys represent a habitat-filtered subset of the
original settling population: individuals that fail to establish or settle are unobserved.
In this conceptualization, habitat effects on coral performance may be expressed primarily
through differential early post-settlement survival rather than through differential growth
among survivors and would not be detectable in growth data derived from established
colonies. It is likely second- and higher-order effects (habitat in combination with other
factors) that are driving outcomes.

These findings highlight the importance of considering the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem
[MAUP, @holtAggregationEcologicalEffects1996; @kwanUncertainGeographicContext2012;
@rileyRealWorldData2024]. Conclusions drawn on one spatial scale do not necessarily transfer
to another, and a model generalized for a region may therefore provide indicative
projections without being applicable to any specific area within it. This interpretation is
broadly consistent with findings from other studies on the GBR, where no single
environmental factor has been identified as a strong predictor of seeded coral performance
[@jurriaansWaveEnergyOther2025]. The spatial resolution of environmental covariates may also
limit what can be resolved from colony-level growth and survival observations. For example,
the modeled eReefs temperature (~1 km) and bottom current speed (10 m) may miss conditions
experienced by individual colonies. Weak sensitivity to these factors likely reflects a
mismatch in measurement scale rather than ecological irrelevance. Together, these results
illustrate how sensitivity analysis can help assess whether available data resolve factors
relevant to the model's intended scale and purpose, while flagging potential limitations.

Generally, colony size is indicated as the dominant factor for predicting annualized
increase in diameter (a proxy for growth) across all examined spatial scales. Diameter is
also among the leading factors for survival, and so provides the primary empirical basis for
the size-structured model design. It leads the survival ranking at Moore Reef, Masig Reef,
and the Torres Strait regionally, while depth ranks marginally ahead of diameter for
survival in the Offshore North region, reflecting the weaker diameter sensitivity of
corymbose Acropora discussed below.

For survival of fast-growing forms such as corymbose *Acropora*, diameter sensitivity was
found to be more variable across locations than for other groups. The influence of diameter
appears weaker at Moore Reef (specifically for corymbose *Acropora*), where temperature (as
indicated by eReefs modelling) and depth are indicated as more influential, whereas diameter
remains the dominant factor for survival at Masig Reef and at the regional scale for the
Torres Strait. A consistent size-structured framework is nonetheless retained across all
groups. Even for fast-growing forms a positive size-survival relationship is present in the
regressions, and a uniform structural approach across groups aids tractability and
cross-group comparison. The structural decisions described in @sec-model-description omit
factors for which available data cannot resolve their influence.

# Model description {#sec-model-description}

Kora is a size-structured model implemented with the high-performance Julia programming
language [@bezansonJuliaFreshApproach2017a]. Coral growth and background mortality are
parameterized directly from field photomosaics and *in situ* juvenile quadrat data
[@australianinstituteofmarinescienceaimsEcoRRAPCoralDemographic2023;
@doropoulosImpactEnvironmentalGradients2025; @gordonFieldPhotogrammetry4D2023;
@toorFieldPhotogrammetry4D2025]. Representation of acute environmental disturbances focused
on marine heatwaves; a key concern under projected climate conditions
[@hendrickxOnlinecouplingWidelyrangedTimescales2021]. The model simulates coral reef
dynamics with comparatively low structural data requirements. Colony diameter provides the
foundation for the model structure, as sensitivity analysis indicates it is the dominant
factor for growth at all examined scales and among the leading factors for survival.

Kora operates on a discrete annual basis, as a continuous representation of intra-annual
dynamics was deemed unnecessary for producing indicative future trajectories. A key
assumption is that background mortality occurs throughout each year, and thus is applied
first to represent the events of the past year. The survivors then go on to reproduce once
they reach maturity, and their progeny settle alongside any corals that are deployed through
anthropogenic intervention. In the GBR, coral spawning occurs over October and November
[@babcockSynchronousSpawnings1051986], prior to peak heatwaves which typically occur over
summer (December - April). As such, heat stress is applied last, the survivors of which then
go on to grow (increase in diameter), with the process repeating until the end of the
simulation.

A representative reef area is modeled, which serves as a proxy for a given locale whether
this be a transect, reef plot, site, or even an entire reef itself. The simulated area
represents a contiguous coral habitable area. Kora is not spatially explicit, and so corals
within the simulated area are assumed to be uniformly distributed and constrained to the
available habitable space. A single model evaluation on a standard laptop can be conducted
in 50 to 100 milliseconds for a representative 288m^2^ area (an area that aligns with
EcoRRAP sites). This performance makes the model suitable for participatory workshop
settings, where decision-maker preferences can be elicited and the implications of
management options explored interactively in near real-time. For a single location and five
functional groups, Kora involves 58 factors, although not all are required to be considered
for a given application. An overview of its computational scalability is offered in
Supplementary A.

Each coral colony is tracked by diameter (cm) and functional group, with the population
capped to a maximum of 20 individuals per m^2^. This is an assumed upper bound. As an
indicative reference point, AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Program data has reported 2.7 - 12.1
juveniles/m^2^ since 2005, with @doropoulosImpactEnvironmentalGradients2025 finding that
recruitment on natural substrates varied between 1 - 5 recruits/m^2^. Elsewhere, regional
juvenile coral densities on natural substrate across the central and western Pacific range
from 1.5 to 10.5 colonies/m^2^ [@couchEcologicalEnvironmentalPredictors2023].

Density-dependent settlement and mortality govern the earliest life stages of coral
populations [@vermeijDENSITYDEPENDENTSETTLEMENTMORTALITY2008], and colony abundance and
cover were highest at intermediate settlement densities, with higher settlement densities
instead leading to overcrowding and reduced long-term survival
[@cameronDensityCoralLarvae2020]. Only a fraction of juveniles would therefore be expected
to survive through to adulthood, placing standing adult colony density well below this
juvenile benchmark. The 20/m^2^ cap sits well above this ceiling, leaving ample headroom for
the tracked population. Space is not explicitly modeled, but growth slows as inhabited area
approaches carrying capacity, the maximum area corals can occupy, capturing larger colonies'
competitive advantage, faster growth, and size-dependent mortality [cf.
@alvarez-noriegaNegligibleEffectCompetition2018; @lecheneLegacyEffectsMild2026] without
spatially explicit tracking.

The case of a single reef area is described here for the purpose of detailing model
implementation. Further details of each constituent model are provided in the corresponding
subsections below. The population state at time $t$ for a given functional group and
spatial location is represented as the indexed multiset of colony diameters:

$$X_{t} = \left\{ d_{i,t}\ :i = 1,\ \ldots,\ \left| X_{t} \right| \right\},\ d_{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$$ {#eq-population-state}

where $d_{i,t}$ is the diameter (in cm) of colony $i$. The temporal dynamics of this
population are then described by:

$$Z_{t} = S_{E}\left( S_{B}\left( X_{t} \right),\ \theta_{t} \right),\ Z_{t} \subseteq X_{t}$$

$$X_{t + 1} = G_{t}\left( Z_{t} \cup R\left( Z_{t} \right) \right) \cup H_{t}$$ {#eq-temporal-dynamics}

$S_{B}$ is a size-dependent background mortality operator that stochastically removes
colonies from $X_{t}$, yielding a subset of survivors. Environmental mortality
$S_{E}( \cdot ,\theta_{t})$ then acts on that subset, where $\theta_{t}$ denotes experienced
degree heating weeks (DHW). Both mortality operators only remove colonies from $X_{t}$.
Colonies that reach and exceed the minimum reproductive size threshold (assumed to be \>
5cm) in $Z_{t}$ contribute to natural recruitment:

$$R\left( Z_{t} \right) = \left\{ d_{j,t}\ :j = 1,\ \ldots,\ n_{r} \right\},\ d_{j,t}\sim N(1.5,0.2)\ truncated\ to\ \lbrack 0.5,\ 2.5\rbrack cm$$ {#eq-recruitment-natural}

where $n_{r}$ is the number of new settlers determined by the reproductive output of mature
colonies in $Z_{t}$. Recruit diameters are drawn from a truncated normal distribution
representing the approximate size range of one-year-old corals.
$H_{t} = \{ d_{k,t}:k = 1,\ldots,n_{h}\}$ is the set of colonies added through anthropogenic
intervention, assumed to settle concurrently with natural recruits. The size-dependent
growth operator $G_{t}$ then advances every colony diameter forward by one timestep:

$$G_{t}(A) = \left\{ g_{t}(d):d \in A \right\},\ g_{t}(d) > d$$ {#eq-growth-operator}

where $g_{t}$ is the functional-group and location-specific growth function, mapping each
colony diameter to its diameter at time $t + 1$.

Coral cover is subsequently estimated from the resulting population:

$$C_{t} = \sum_{i = 1}^{|X_{t}|}{\frac{{\pi\left( d_{i,t} \right)}^{2}}{4} \cdot \kappa,\ d_{i,t} \in X_{t}}$$ {#eq-coral-cover}

where $C_{t}$ is the projected planar cover (m^2^). The $\kappa$ scaling coefficient
converts cover estimates from cm^2^ to m^2^ (i.e., $\kappa ≔ 1/10000$). It is explicitly
shown here to indicate that any spatial unit of interest is supported. The model then
enables emergent behavior to occur as the functional groups are differentiated, and
community composition of both coral groups and their size distributions are explicitly
modeled.

## Functional groups {#sec-functional-groups}

Kora categorizes coral species into five functional groups based on morphology and life
history traits. Representing corals by their functional forms captures their interactions
and key life history trade-offs that govern reef dynamics to enable future exploration of
the impact on coral diversity. The functional groups currently simulated by Kora represent
the dominant growth forms (at least 80% of hard coral abundance) across sampled reefs and
habitats. It is acknowledged here that the selection is non-exhaustive and misses key
functional groups, such as staghorn and bottlebrush *Acropora*, branching Porites and
foliose corals.

+--------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+
| **Functional Group**                       | **Description**                            |
+:===========================================+:===========================================+
| tabular *Acropora*                         | Fast-growing plate-like colonies that      |
|                                            | dominate in low-disturbance conditions     |
+--------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+
| corymbose *Acropora*                       | Moderately fast-growing compact branching  |
|                                            | colonies, including caespitose, corymbose, |
|                                            | or digitate morphology.                    |
+--------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+
| branching non-*Acropora*                   | Branching forms with intermediate growth   |
|                                            | rates such as *Pocillopora* spp.           |
+--------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+
| Small massives                             | Slower-growing, more robust forms that     |
|                                            | grow to a maximum of \~50cm diameter.      |
|                                            | This group includes massive and sub-massive|
|                                            | colonies.                                  |
|                                            | Exemplar genera include *Goniastrea* and   |
|                                            | *Platygyra*.                               |
+--------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+
| Large massives                             | Capable of growing to very large diameters |
|                                            | albeit slowly; most resistant to           |
|                                            | heat disturbance. This group includes      |
|                                            | massive and sub-massive colonies.          |
|                                            | Currently represents                       |
|                                            | Porites species complex only.              |
+--------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+

: Description of represented functional groups. See @stbl-12 and @stbl-11 for the taxa and
benthic classes assigned to each group. {#tbl-2}

## Constituent model development {#sec-model-development}

Kora is composed of five constituent models, each representing a key demographic process:
growth (@sec-growth-models), survival (@sec-survival-models), bleaching mortality
(@sec-bleaching-mortality), recruitment (@sec-recruitment), and thermal adaptation
(@sec-thermal-adaptation). Growth and survival are represented as continuous regressions
fitted directly to field-derived annualized rates, whereas bleaching mortality, recruitment,
and thermal adaptation draw on published empirical relationships and mechanistic
representations of the underlying processes, reflecting the more limited availability of
direct field observations for calibrating these dynamics. Both growth and survival
regressions were assessed via an identical training (60%) / test (40%) split of the
available data.

### Growth models {#sec-growth-models}

Linear regressions were fitted to annualized colony growth derived from orthorectified
photomosaics (described in @sec-model-development-workflow) using ordinary least
squares. Fitting directly to observation pairs would introduce temporal bias, as observed
growth increments occurred at different time scales while the model operates on one-year
timesteps. To address this bias, the annualized growth rate for each observation pair was
estimated via Euler approximation. While prior research has documented logistic (asymptotic)
growth patterns in coral planar area over colony lifespans, the linear approach captures
observed growth dynamics within the size ranges and timeframes of monitoring data.

The annualization took the approach:

$${d'}_{t + 1} = d_{t_{obs}^{-}} + {(d_{t_{obs}^{+}} - d}_{t_{obs}^{-}})/(\frac{\Delta t_{obs}}{365.25})$$ {#eq-growth-annualized}

where:

- ${d'}_{t + 1}$ is the estimated diameter after one year of growth

- $d_{t_{obs}^{-}}$ is the previous observation

- $d_{t_{obs}^{+}}$ is the next observation

- $\Delta t_{obs}$ is the number of days between observations

- $365.25$ is a constant for the mean number of days per year accounting for leap years

Annualized diameter (${d'}_{t + 1}$) is then a function of initial diameter
$d_{t_{obs}^{-}}$, which was subsequently applied in a yearly difference equation. Sampling
of coral sizes occurred during the Austral summer to ensure growth rates are seasonally
consistent. The resulting model coefficients are shown in @stbl-3.

Predictive performance on held-out test data was strong for all groups (@stbl-4), with
Root Mean Square Errors (RMSE) ranging from 1.02 - 3.91 cm and
Pearson correlation between 0.87 - 0.997. Performance was generally consistent between
training and test datasets, with two out of five groups showing equal or better test RMSE,
indicating no systematic overfitting. High rank-order correlations (Kendall's τ ≥ 0.71
for all groups) and low RMSE relative to size ranges demonstrate that models reliably
predict relative growth rates, a critical requirement for projecting population-level
dynamics. Growth model performance for tabular *Acropora* is shown in @fig-4, with
similar figures for all other functional groups found in Supplementary E.

![Indicative performance for tabular Acropora ("Acro Table") at Moore Reef for
both training and test datasets. See supplementary materials for regression plots for all
modeled functional groups and their
coefficients.](../figs/regressions/offshore_north/moore/growth_acro_table.png){#fig-4 width="6.268054461942257in"
height="2.0893514873140857in"}

Growth ($G$) is conceptualized as being moderated by two key factors: space constraints and
location-specific scalers. Here, growth is increasingly constrained as the area covered by
corals approaches available space, following a logistic function:

$$G_{modified} = 1\ /\ \lbrack 1 + e^{k\left( \frac{C_{t}}{K} - \tau_{0} \right)}\rbrack$$ {#eq-growth-space-constraint}

where $G_{modified}$ is a dimensionless multiplier that reduces from 1 to 0 as coral cover
approaches the available space; $C_{t}$ is the current cover (at time $t$), $K$ is the
carrying capacity of the represented area, $\tau_{0}$ represents the inflection point at
which space constraints become significant and growth is reduced by 50%; nominally set to
0.96. How rapidly growth is constrained is controlled by $k$ which is nominally set to 20.

Location and functional group specific scalers ($\alpha_{f,l}$) allow for spatial
heterogeneity in growth rates due to local environmental conditions, support calibration
processes and, critically, enable integration with additional representation of
environmental factors:

$$G\left( d_{t + 1} \right) = d_{t} + \lbrack f_{g}\left( d_{t} \right) \cdot G_{modified} \cdot \alpha_{f,l}\rbrack$$ {#eq-growth-spatial}

such that the model projects diameter at time $t + 1$ based on the growth for each
functional group ($f_{g}$):

$$f_{g}\left( d_{t} \right) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\ln(d_{t})$$ {#eq-diameter-growth}

Growth predictions are capped to the largest observed diameter. This is not explicitly
detailed in the equations above as it may be desirable to allow extrapolation to represent
larger corals.

### Survival models {#sec-survival-models}

Background survival ($S_{B}$) is conceptualized as a stochastic binary process where a
colony survives or dies completely. It is a function of colony diameter at time of
observation and is determined by comparing a random draw $U\sim Uniform(0,1)$ against
size-dependent probability ($S_{\mathcal{l}}$):

$$\begin{aligned}
S_{\mathcal{l}}(d) &= \min(1, \max(0, \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\ln(d) + \beta_{2}\ln(d)^{2})) \\
S_{B}(d) &= d \cdot 1_{U < S_{\mathcal{l}}(d)}
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-survival-background}

The polynomial is clamped to $[0, 1]$ to guard against extrapolation beyond the range of the
training data producing non-physical probabilities. The indicator $1_{U <
S_{\mathcal{l}}(d)}$ evaluates to zero for colonies that do not survive, setting their
diameter to zero within the timestep; these zero-diameter entries are filtered from the
population before advancing to the next timestep (see @eq-temporal-dynamics).

Second-degree polynomials were fitted to size-binned annualized survival probabilities. For
each bin, survival was estimated under a constant-hazard (exponential survival) model.
Colonies were pooled by total colony-days at risk (hazard = deaths / colony-days),
annualized as $\exp(-\text{hazard} \times 365.25)$, rather than by a simple average of raw
survival/death outcomes to avoid conflating colonies observed over short intervals with high
survival, since exposure time to risk differs across observation pairs. Bin-level
variability was estimated via bootstrap standard error of this annualized estimate
(resampling colonies, preserving each colony's survival/interval pairing), providing an
indication of variability of survival across diameter space. Data for each functional group
was partitioned into unequal sized bins, applying the same size-stratified adaptive quantile
binning method used for the empirical sensitivity analysis. Details are found in
[Supplementary D: Adaptive Quantile Binning
method](#supplementary-d-adaptive-quantile-binning-method).

Background survival generally increases with size, reflecting the greater resilience of
larger colonies [@hughest.p.PopulationDynamicsBased1984;
@madinMechanicalVulnerabilityExplains2014; @connellPOPULATIONECOLOGYREEFBUILDING1973]. The
resulting model coefficients are found in @stbl-5. Predictive performance showed different
patterns across morphological groups (see @stbl-6); low test RMSE scores (ranging from 0.028
to 0.068 across bin means) were nonetheless found. Performance for tabular *Acropora* is
shown in @fig-5.

Coral survival for the large massive functional group exhibited strong size-dependence (test
Pearson = 0.91), with survival probability increasing predictably with colony diameter and a
high rank-order correlation (Kendall's τ = 0.83). Small massives showed a weaker
relationship (test Pearson = 0.71, Kendall's τ = 0.57). Tabular *Acropora* showed weaker
size-dependent survival (test Pearson = 0.60, Kendall's τ = 0.001). Its fast-growing,
fragmentation-prone morphology is exposed to mortality from storms, predation, and
competition [@madinMechanicalVulnerabilityExplains2014;
@moraisDangerousDemographicsPostbleach2021; @speareSizedependentMortalityCorals2022].

These stochastic processes are generally not readily predicted from size alone, however, and
are subject to environmental and ecological processes that are highly location specific.
Group-level sensitivity analyses reflect this pattern: corymbose *Acropora* survival shows
weaker initial diameter sensitivity at Moore Reef, where eReefs temperature and depth are
indicated as more influential, consistent with the lower regression performance for that
group. A compensating scaling term for the spatial area of interest partially accounts for
the influence of these unincorporated environmental factors. The corresponding design
trade-off is explored in the Discussion (@sec-discussion).

![Survival regression for tabular *Acropora* at Moore Reef. Observations are split
into 10 bins, where points indicate bin mean and its whiskers indicate bin size. Shaded area
indicates $\pm$ 1 bootstrapped standard error (of the annualized survival estimate, 1000 replicates).
Uncertainty varies with diameter, as indicated by the variation in survival probability, particularly
in the lower diameters.](../figs/regressions/offshore_north/moore/survival_acro_table.png){#fig-5 width="6.82886154855643in"
height="2.2762871828521436in"}

### Bleaching mortality {#sec-bleaching-mortality}

Mortality from thermal stress is the primary environmental stressor represented in Kora as
it is the dominant driver of coral mortality under projected climate conditions. Degree
Heating Week (DHW; °C-weeks and denoted here as $\theta$) indicates the cumulative heat
stress through the accumulation of daily temperatures exceeding 1°C above the local
long-term maximum summer temperature over the preceding 12 weeks
[@kayanneValidationDegreeHeating2017a]. Values greater than 4.0 °C-weeks are thought to
induce bleaching, and those above 8.0 °C-weeks are said to induce widespread bleaching and
some mortality [@hughesGlobalWarmingTransforms2018]. Other exogenous shocks, such as cyclones
or ship strikes, outbreaks of Crown-of-Thorns Seastars and other predation
or spread of disease are not explicitly represented.

Bleaching mortality is implemented as deterministic partial mortality, where each colony's
diameter is reduced proportionally to its mortality risk. The approach reflects observed
bleaching responses where colonies may partially survive. Population-level susceptibility is
determined by the population's thermal tolerance distribution. Depth amelioration (see
@eq-depth-amelioration below) is first applied to the experienced DHW to obtain the
effective thermal stress:

$$\theta_{eff} = \theta \cdot \alpha_{depth}$$ {#eq-dhw-depth-adjusted}

For a given effective DHW ($\theta_{eff}$), the proportion of the population affected
($P_{affected}$) is given as:

$$P_{affected} = F(\theta_{eff} \mid \ \mu_{\theta tol},\ \sigma_{\theta tol})$$ {#eq-bleaching-affected}

where $F$ is the CDF of a truncated normal distribution with mean $\mu_{tol}$ and standard
deviation $\sigma_{tol}$, truncated at $\theta$ = 4 (the threshold where bleaching typically
begins) and $\mu_{\theta tol} + 10$. The upper bound of the distribution can therefore shift
over time. The implementation presented here assumes only corals at or above their
functional group's reproductive maturity size threshold (5cm diameter) are susceptible to
bleaching [@depczynskiBleachingCoralMortality2013; @speareSizedependentMortalityCorals2022].
The representation here is a deliberate simplification; there is recent
evidence that size-based bleaching can be taxon and severity dependent [@burnDifferentialBleachingSusceptibility2023; @alvarez-noriegaContrastingPatternsChanges2018].
See @sec-thermal-adaptation on thermal adaptation for further details.

Size-dependent susceptibility to bleaching is incorporated with:

$$S_{size}(d) = 1\ /\ (1 + e^{k(d - d_{0})})$$ {#eq-bleaching-size-dependent}

where $k$ controls steepness as with for growth (nominally set to 0.15) and $d_{0} ≔ 150$
(in cm) assumed to be the size at which colonies become substantially more resistant to heat
stress.

Depth amelioration follows empirical relationships from @bairdDeclineBleachingSuggests2018:

$$\alpha_{depth} = \text{max(}0\text{, min(}1,\ e^{- 0.07551(\delta - 2)}\text{))}$$ {#eq-depth-amelioration}

where $\delta$ is depth in meters, capturing the protective effect of depth on thermal
stress. Depth amelioration is applied directly to the experienced DHW
($\theta_{eff} = \theta \cdot \alpha_{depth}$) before computing population susceptibility,
ensuring that colonies at depth experience proportionally reduced thermal stress.

The realized mortality for an individual colony is:

$$M_{bleach}(d,\ \theta,\delta) = P_{affected} \cdot S_{size}(d)$$ {#eq-bleaching-mortality-realized}

Survival from bleaching ($S_{E}$) is then:

$$S_{E}(d,\theta,\delta) = d \cdot \left\lbrack 1 - M_{bleach}(d,\theta,\delta) \right\rbrack^{0.5}$$ {#eq-bleaching-survival}

The square-root exponent converts an area-based mortality estimate into the equivalent linear (diameter)
reduction, since area scales with the square of diameter. Modeled individuals represent a unit of coral
area within a functional group rather than a single biological colony. The represented
diameter reduction therefore captures partial loss of that area unit, whether this reflects
shrinkage of one colony, loss of fragments, or mortality of contributing sub-colonies.

Critically, the modeled accuracy of bleaching mortality is highly sensitive
to the assumed depth, quality of DHW predictions and how they were downscaled to the area of
interest. The empirical relationship determined by @bairdDeclineBleachingSuggests2018 was
also drawn from analyses using data across the northern GBR. While potentially adjusted by
the DHW tolerance mechanism described above, it may over-represent bleaching mortality.

Applying mortality as a proportional reduction in diameter produces a stronger penalty on
coral cover than an equivalent rate of total colony mortality, as cover scales with the
square of diameter. The implementation therefore represents a conservative upper bound on
bleaching-driven cover loss, consistent with the objective of assessing reef state under
disturbed conditions.

### Recruitment {#sec-recruitment}

Larval production (fecundity) is modeled as a power-law function of colony size as in
@hallReproductiveStrategiesModular1996:

$$L_{\text{prod}}(d,\ f) = a_{f} \cdot d^{b_{f}}$$ {#eq-larval-production}

where $a_{f}$ and $b_{f}$ are functional group-specific parameters. Only colonies above
maturity thresholds (assumed to be 5cm diameter) contribute to reproduction. The parameter
$a_{f}$ ranges from 0.15 to 0.5 with higher values reflecting a greater per-area
reproductive output. The exponent $b_{f}$ is set to 2.0 for all groups, approximating the
relationship between colony area and reproductive potential.

Larval connectivity is incorporated via both local retention and external supply. A
proportion of produced larvae (from $L_{\text{prod}}(d,f)$) is assumed to settle at their
origin, representing self-recruitment [nominally set to 0.3, cf.
@hockConnectivitySystemicResilience2017]. The remainder are assumed to disperse elsewhere.
In the single location case, this value could be adjusted to reflect influx from other
locations under the assumption that the maximum larval pool is reflective of local ecosystem
state. The simplification captures the essential dynamics of larval retention which could be
informed by estimates from a hydrodynamic dispersal model. In this case, the nominal value
was selected based on prior analyses [@hockConnectivitySystemicResilience2017].

Settlement success is density and space dependent, following:

$$R(l,f) = \text{min}\!\left(A_{l} \cdot D_{\text{max}},\ L_{\text{set},l,f}\right)$$ {#eq-settlement-success}

where:

- $K_{l}$ is the location's carrying capacity

- $C_{l}$ is the current coral cover at location $l$

- $A_{l}$ is the available space, computed as the carrying capacity minus current cover:
  $A_{l} = K_{l} - C_{l}$

- $D_{\text{max}}$ is the maximum settler density during recruitment. This represents the
  constraint on new recruits settling per unit area during each recruitment event, and is
  distinct from the overall population density cap of 20 individuals per m² that applies to
  the total population at any location.

- $L_{\text{set},l,f}$ is the larval supply available for settlement at location $l$ for
  functional group $f$, derived from larval production $L_{\text{prod}}(d,f)$ after applying
  self-seeding and dispersal losses

- $R(l,f)$ is the recruitment function, determining the number of successful settlers of
  functional group $f$ at location $l$

The distinction between larval production $L_{\text{prod}}(d,f)$ and larval supply
$L_{\text{set},l,f}$ reflects the model's treatment of connectivity: production is the total
fecundity of mature colonies, while supply is the larval pool available at each location
after accounting for local self-retention (0.3) and external dispersal. The formulation
ensures that recruitment success is modulated by available space, with settlement declining
as cover approaches carrying capacity. The recruits per m^2^ respect estimated density
thresholds, and that total settlement cannot exceed the available larval supply. Recruits
enter with diameters drawn from a normal distribution (mean 1.5 cm, standard deviation 0.2
cm) truncated to the range \[0.5, 2.5\] cm.

### Thermal adaptation {#sec-thermal-adaptation}

Kora incorporates a quantitative framework to represent thermal adaptation across
generations to enable exploration of localized interventions under different climate
scenarios. Interventions refer to the "seeding" of coral through assisted migration or
transplantation, or aquacultural means, including those which may be thermally enhanced to
have higher tolerances to heat stress [cf. @doropoulosImpactEnvironmentalGradients2025].
Although the examples here do not explore projections into future environmental and
management conditions, how such mechanisms are incorporated is detailed for completeness.

Rather than tracking individual genotypes explicitly, the model represents thermal tolerance
as a quantitative trait following a normal distribution within each population. This is
consistent with empirical dose-response assays of critical DHW bleaching/mortality
thresholds across coral colonies, which report substantial but bounded within-population
variability characterizable by a mean and standard deviation [e.g., 6.7 $\pm$ 1.1 °C-weeks
across colonies; @lachsNoApparentTradeoffs2023]. The implementation adapts prior efforts
described in @ribeirodealmeidaCoralBloxComputationallyEfficient2026 to consider the
size-structured approach implemented in Kora.

The inheritance of thermal tolerance assumes entirely random population mixing (panmictic
reproduction), selection only during thermal stress events, and that the response to
selection is determined solely by heritable additive genetic effects. These processes
operate at each time step, allowing populations to evolve in response to thermal stress.
Each location and functional group maintain two distinct populations: wild corals and
deployed corals that are aquaculturally cultivated and/or thermally enhanced. Both
populations are characterized by their thermal tolerance distributions with mean $\mu_{tol}$
and standard deviation $\sigma_{tol}$. Thermally tolerant corals are assumed to have similar
growth rates and vulnerability to other stressors as wild corals.

Each functional group maintains a tolerance distribution:

$$\theta_{t,tol}\sim N(\mu_{tol,t},\ \sigma_{tol,t})$$ {#eq-thermal-tolerance-dist}

Values for $\mu$ and $\sigma$ may both shift over time. During bleaching events ($\theta >
4$, see @sec-bleaching-mortality on bleaching mortality for details) the mean tolerance
shifts as smaller, less heat-tolerant corals are disproportionately affected, and $\sigma$
narrows toward the truncated distribution of survivors, reflecting the loss of the least
heat-tolerant individuals from the population. $\sigma$ is floored to avoid collapsing
toward zero under repeated bleaching events. On recruitment, $\sigma$ is blended back toward
each functional group's founder spread in proportion to the number of recruits relative to
the existing mature population, restoring variance after a strong post-disturbance
recruitment pulse. The mean tolerance of parents at time $t$ is determined by weighted
cover:

$$\mu_{tol,t} = \frac{C_{wild,t} \cdot \mu_{wild,t} + C_{deployed,t} \cdot \mu_{deployed,t}}{C_{wild,t} + C_{deployed,t}}$$ {#eq-thermal-tolerance-mean}

Where $C$ represents population cover, as it is assumed that reproductive success is
proportional to area covered. In this way, limited intervention in areas with high wild
larval supply will have limited evolutionary impact through genetic swamping.

New recruits then inherit tolerances from parents according to the breeder's equation
[@lernerGeneticBasisSelection1958; @lushAnimalBreedingPlans1943]:

$$\mu_{recruits,t} = \mu_{tol,\ t - 2} + h^{2} \cdot \Delta_{\text{sel}}$$ {#eq-breeders-equation}

where $h^{2} = 0.3$ and represents the narrow-sense heritability of coral thermal tolerance
and $\Delta_{\text{sel}} = \mu_{tol,t - 1} - \mu_{tol,t - 2}$, representing the change in
the mean phenotype of the parent population compared to the offspring; also referred to as
the selection differential. Here, $\mu_{tol,t - 1}$ and $\mu_{tol,t - 2}$ represent the
thermal tolerance of the existing population (parents) at time $t - 1$ and $t - 2$,
respectively.

The nominal heritability value ($h²\ = \ 0.3$) reflects empirical estimates from coral
thermal tolerance studies [@bairos-novakCoralAdaptationClimate2021;
@humanesSelectiveBreedingEnhances2024]. Lower heritability values imply slower evolutionary
responses, as phenotypic variation is dominated by environmental or non-additive genetic
effects. Higher heritability would accelerate adaptation but may be unrealistic for traits
under historical selection.

This univariate Breeder's equation-based approach makes several simplifying assumptions
[@morrisseyDangerApplyingBreeders2010]: thermal tolerance is the only trait associated with
fitness and is normally distributed, heritability is constant across environments [although
they differ across functional groups; @visscherHeritabilityGenomicsEra2008], there are no
genetic correlations with other fitness-related traits [similar to
@lachsNoApparentTradeoffs2023], and selection acts only through survival rather than
fecundity differences. These assumptions are justified for shorter management timescales
[@coulsonPredictingEvolutionMultiple2021], where evolutionary dynamics are dominated by
responses to selection making use of standing variation rather than new (de novo) mutations
[@barrettAdaptationStandingGenetic2008; @matuszewskiCatchMeIf2015]. Prior
assessments applying similar approaches have also demonstrated the insensitivity of outcomes
to the parameterization of heritability within a projected time frame of \~75 years [cf.
@ribeirodealmeidaCoralBloxComputationallyEfficient2026; @bozecRapidlyClosingWindow2025].

+--------------------------+----------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Functional Group**     | **Mean tolerance           | **Standard Deviation           |
|                          | (**$\mathbf{\mu}$**)**     | (**$\mathbf{\sigma}$**)**      |
+:=========================+===========================:+===============================:+
| tabular *Acropora*       | 3.75                       | 2.9                            |
+--------------------------+----------------------------+--------------------------------+
| corymbose *Acropora*     | 4.08                       | 3.16                           |
+--------------------------+----------------------------+--------------------------------+
| branching non-*Acropora* | 4.49                       | 3.47                           |
+--------------------------+----------------------------+--------------------------------+
| small massives           | 6.17                       | 4.77                           |
+--------------------------+----------------------------+--------------------------------+
| large massives           | 7.15                       | 5.54                           |
+--------------------------+----------------------------+--------------------------------+

: Assumed initial thermal tolerance values for each functional group. {#tbl-3}

# Example applications

Two reefs, in the Offshore Northern region (Moore Reef, 16-071) and Torres Strait (Masig
Reef), were selected to demonstrate Kora. Models for both reefs were configured to represent
a 288m^2^ area at an assumed average depth of 9m. The conceptualized area roughly aligns
with four 72m^2^ plots as per EcoRRAP monitoring practices, and assumes the represented area
is suitable for coral settlement. The demonstration illustrates Kora's ability to provide an
indication of reef state based on available data, primarily in terms of percent coral cover
and the contribution to this by the represented functional groups. It is acknowledged that
in practice coral cover is not the only metric of concern
[@mcwilliamCapturingDimensionsCoral2026; @tanADRIAIndicatorsJuliaPackage2026;
@lachsRisingCoverPopulation2025; @gonzalez-riveroCoralCoverFramework2025]. For each reef, an
ensemble of potential parameterizations that best characterize observations are developed
through a multi-start evolutionary optimization approach.

Moore Reef is a popular tourist destination and has been well-studied, with LTMP monitoring
beginning in 1989. Cyclone Joy, however, struck the reef in 1990, with the next available
manta-tow observation recorded in 1994. Moore Reef has approximately 17.57km^2^ of coral
habitable area [@bozecRapidlyClosingWindow2025;
@iwanagaGbrrestorationCanonicalreefsCanonical2025]. LTMP manta-tow observations around the
reef perimeter were complemented with available EcoRRAP orthorectified photogrammetry data.
Manta-tow data was used to provide an indicative estimate of coral cover, whereas EcoRRAP
data (at specific reef plots) was adopted to provide estimates of relative functional group
abundance. A key assumption is that these data are sufficiently representative of Moore Reef
as a whole.

Due to the difficulty in representing the impact of cyclones, the simulated timeframe
spanned 1994 (the next available survey year after Cyclone Joy) to 2023, with 10 LTMP
observations between 1994 and 2021 used for calibration. Observations following the 2017
bleaching event (2018 and 2020) were withheld to allow assessment of post-disturbance
model behavior. EcoRRAP estimates of functional group abundance for 2021 were used in the
calibration process, while 2022 and 2023 were reserved for validation.

Masig Reef is in the central Torres Strait and is estimated to have 0.46km^2^ of coral
habitable area [@bozecRapidlyClosingWindow2025;
@iwanagaGbrrestorationCanonicalreefsCanonical2025]. In contrast to Moore Reef, there are no
available LTMP observations for Masig Reef. Model assessment adopts available
photogrammetry-derived estimates. The reef was selected to assess model performance and
behavior under data-limited conditions. The available data covers the period between 2021
and 2024. The first three years were used for calibration, with the remaining
year used to assess ensemble trajectories. Masig Reef has no recorded disturbances during
the monitored period, although DHW values are comparatively high over the observation
period, easing only in 2024.

## Ensemble generation

Evolutionary optimization with the Adaptive Differential Evolution
[@feldtRobertfeldtBlackBoxOptimjl2023; @zhangAdaptiveDifferentialEvolution2009] was applied
to identify parameter combinations (i.e., a parameter set) capable of reproducing observed
coral cover dynamics. The resulting ensemble was then assessed to explore the extent to
which parameters were identifiable. Ensemble approaches are commonly applied to identify
model parameterizations that best explain observed system behavior given the uncertainties
involved [@nearingEnsemblesVsInformation2018; @vollertUnlockingEnsembleEcosystem2024].

Evolutionary optimization methods apply concepts of evolutionary theory, maintaining a
population of model parameterizations which are "evolved" towards combinations that best
match observed system behavior through mutation, crossover, and selection. A subset of model
factors was used for this process (outlined in @tbl-4). Growth rates were
adjusted via scaling factors; however, a decision was made not to treat survival rates
similarly, to limit interacting and compensatory behavior that would reduce model
interpretability.
