: Considered parameters and their bounds for the purpose of calibration/training. {#tbl-4}

Bounds are given per reef where they differ, and as a single range where the two reefs share
the same bound. In the Masig bounds, Tab, Cor, Branch, Sm, and Lg denote tabular
*Acropora*, corymbose *Acropora*, branching non-*Acropora*, small massives, and
large massives, respectively. The proportion bounds constrain latent values, which are mapped
through a Gamma(1) quantile and normalized to sum to one; realized proportions may therefore lie
slightly outside the listed bounds. Growth scalers for Masig Reef were fixed at effectively 1.0 (not calibrated)
rather than merely tightened, reflecting a deliberate decision that the reef's smaller area
and EcoRRAP-derived growth curves already encode reef-specific rates. Moore Reef's scalers
were initially fixed on the same reasoning but were reverted to a free range after
diagnostic testing showed this suppressed fit quality and materially altered the sensitivity
ranking (see below and Discussion). This indicates the scalers perform a corrective function
for Moore Reef rather than being redundant; the pattern of correction did not cleanly follow
the tabular/non-tabular morphology split initially hypothesized.

Performance of each ensemble member (a candidate) was ascertained by an objective function
producing values between $0$ and $\infty$, where zero indicates perfect fit (further detail
in @sec-performance-metrics). Candidates were identified through an iterative multi-start
process, using a fitness threshold ($J \leq 0.2$ for Moore Reef, $J \leq 0.3$ for Masig
Reef) to identify 250 viable candidates that exhibit desirable model behavior, forming the
reported ensemble directly. The calibration process was repeated multiple times with
different initializations, with each attempt contributing candidates below the fitness
threshold. Both reefs used a differential evolution population size of 100, retaining each
trial's best 10 below-threshold candidates, with each trial assigned an independent,
trial-specific random seed for model stochasticity. The approach echoes the Pattern-Oriented
Modelling approach of @grimmPatternorientedModellingPopulation1996, as the aim is to
identify parameterizations that reproduce observed system behavior. The ensemble was then
used to assess identifiability of factors found to be influential through sensitivity
analysis.

Parameter influence on calibration fitness ($J$) was assessed with PAWN (@eq-pawn) under two
sampling designs, each of 8,192 samples: unconstrained and constrained. In the unconstrained
analysis, functional-group proportions were sampled uniformly over all possible compositions
(a flat Dirichlet distribution), and all other parameters were sampled within the calibration
bounds (@tbl-4). The unconstrained analysis therefore indicates parameter influence when
nothing is known about community composition. In the constrained analysis, every parameter
was sampled uniformly within the range spanned by the calibrated ensemble, with sampled
functional group proportions renormalized to sum to one. Parameters were sampled
independently within these ranges, whereas good fits require the correlated parameter
combinations the ensemble identified. No constrained sample reached the calibration fitness
threshold (best $J$ of 0.48 at Moore Reef and 0.46 at Masig Reef, against thresholds of 0.2
and 0.3), so the constrained analysis describes parameter influence in the region around the
ensemble rather than within the set of well-fitting parameterizations itself.

The influence of recruitment on coral cover over time was assessed for Moore Reef with a
paired design. Each of the 8,192 samples from the constrained sensitivity analysis was
simulated twice, once with the recruitment parameters as sampled and once with both
recruitment pathways set to zero. Each pair shared the same random number stream, so that
differences between the two runs reflect recruitment alone. PAWN indices relative to a dummy
factor were then calculated for each year on simulated total coral cover in each scenario,
and on the difference between the two (recruitment-attributable cover).

## Performance metrics {#sec-performance-metrics}

The adopted composite metric ($J$) was:

$$J\left( y,\widehat{y} \right) = \left(\tilde{r} + \alpha + L_B\right) + W_{E} + \phi_{f}\left( x_{f} \right) + \rho_{\log}$$ {#eq-composite-metric}

The core term $(\tilde{r} + \alpha + L_B)$ decomposes performance into correlation,
variability, and bias, identical to the Kling-Gupta Efficiency
[@guptaDecompositionMeanSquared2009]. Here, each component is individually normalized to
$[0, 1)$ before summation, giving a core loss bounded within $[0, 3)$. A value of zero
would indicate perfect agreement for all three components. The normalization approach was
inspired by @nossentApplicationNormalizedNashSutcliffe2012. Each component is defined as:

$$\tilde{r} = \frac{1 - r\left(y,\widehat{y}\right)}{2}$$ {#eq-loss-correlation}

$$\alpha = \frac{\left|v - 1\right|}{1 + \left|v - 1\right|}, \quad v = \frac{\sigma(\widehat{y})}{\sigma(y)}$$ {#eq-loss-variability}

$$L_B = \frac{\left|B - 1\right|}{1 + \left|B - 1\right|}, \quad B = \frac{\mu(\widehat{y})}{\mu(y)}$$ {#eq-loss-bias}

where $r$ is the Pearson correlation coefficient, $v$ is the variability ratio, and $B$ is
the bias ratio. $\mu$ and $\sigma$ denote mean and standard deviation. The $u / (1 + u)$
normalization maps each raw deviation $u \in [0,\infty)$ to $[0, 1)$, preventing any single
component from dominating the objective when others are well-constrained. The absolute
values on $v$ and $B$ ensure those metrics treat over- and under-estimation symmetrically.
The correlation component $\tilde{r}$ asymmetrically penalizes anti-correlated predictions
(loss of 1.0) more heavily than uncorrelated predictions (loss of 0.5), reflecting the
expectation that trend reversals are more problematic than magnitude deviations. Additional
weight was placed on the extrema of the time series ($W_{E}$), a penalty term for functional
group cover trajectories ($\phi_{f}(x_{f})$), and alignment with observed benthic community
composition ($\rho_{\log}$), each described below. Observations ($y$) are compared with
modeled outputs ($\widehat{y}$).

Further weight on the initial timestep (denoted as $W_{E}$) is placed to reward candidates
that initialize closer to the observed mean coral cover at the start of the simulation. This is
accomplished by the addition of the Absolute Error calculated using the data points for the
extremes of each time series (i.e., 1 and $N$, the initial year and last year of
observations used for training):

$$W_{E} = (\left| y_{1} - {\widehat{y}}_{1} \right| + \left| y_{N} - {\widehat{y}}_{N} \right|)$$ {#eq-weighted-extrema}

Additionally, parameterizations which drove one or more functional groups to local
extinction within the observation timeframe were considered implausible. To penalize such
parameterizations, a group cover penalty term ($\phi_{f}(x_{f})$) was incorporated. This was
the sum of the number of functional groups which contributed less than 1% of total coral
cover for more than three timesteps.

For timesteps where EcoRRAP-derived data were available, the mean Pearson correlation
coefficient was calculated between log-transformed simulated and observed covers for each
functional group:

$$\rho_{\log} = \left\{ \begin{array}{rlr}
 & \left( \frac{1}{T_{E}} \right)\sum_{t}^{}\left\lbrack 1 - r\left( \log\left( \widehat{x_{f,t}} \right),\log\left( x_{f,t} \right) \right) \right\rbrack\  & \ if\ all\ \widehat{x_{f}} > 0 \\
 & \ 2z_{f}\  & otherwise
\end{array} \right.\ $$ {#eq-correlation-functional-group}

where $\widehat{x_{f}}$ and $x_{f}$ represent simulated and observed abundances for the
represented functional groups ($f$). Here, $t$ is the timestep, and $T_{E}$ is the number of
EcoRRAP observation timesteps. Using the log transform emphasizes proportional relationships
rather than absolute magnitudes to ensure the relative rankings in terms of abundance align
with observations. The metric is converted to a distance measure (subtracting correlation
from 1.0) such that values approaching zero indicate better alignment of functional group
composition patterns. If any zero values are encountered in the simulated time series of
functional group cover ($z_{f}$), twice the number of zeros is assigned to heavily penalize
such parameterizations.

Through this composite metric the training process considers timing, correlation and bias
with respect to observed coral cover [the Normalised Kling-Gupta Efficiency, or NKGE;
@nossentApplicationNormalizedNashSutcliffe2012; @guptaDecompositionMeanSquared2009], initial
and final reef state within the calibration period (with $W_{E}$) and considers plausibility
of functional group trajectories (via $\phi(x_{f})$ and $\rho_{\log}$). A consequence of
this formulation is reduced interpretability, as the metric is bounded between 0 and $+
\infty$.

For simplicity, model performance is reported using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) for coral
cover and log-correlation to indicate alignment with estimated relative abundances. As an
error metric, RMSE values closer to zero indicate increased agreement with LTMP estimates of
coral cover. Log-correlation is reported as the mean of the Pearson correlation ($r$)
between log-transformed simulated and observed functional group abundances across
observations:

$$r_{\text{Pearson,log}} = \frac{1}{T_{E}}\Sigma_{t}\lbrack r\left( \log\left( \widehat{x_{f,t}} \right),\log\left( x_{f,t} \right) \right)\rbrack$$ {#eq-log-correlation}

Values closer to 1.0 indicate group-level abundances proportionally align with
photogrammetry-derived estimates. These metrics are used to assess both the best fit
(highest performing ensemble member) as well as the ensemble mean. The latter being a simple
aggregate measure shown to provide good performance for the purpose of projections
[@wangComparisonHydrologicalModel2021a; @willcockEnsemblesEcosystemService2020a].

# Results {#sec-results}

For Moore Reef, the ensemble reproduced historic cover dynamics with ensemble mean RMSE of
\~1.26% for the calibration years and \~1.50% for validation (@fig-6; full ensemble
trajectory detailed in @sfig-3). The ensemble reveals characteristic dynamics:
faster-growing corals (particularly corymbose *Acropora*) dominate pre-bleaching
trajectories, while massives are relatively more abundant post-bleaching. This follows
established understanding of the lower susceptibility to bleaching and slower competitive
recovery of massive growth forms [@moraisDangerousDemographicsPostbleach2021;
@pratchettContrastingShiftsCoral2020]. Small and large massives combined represented an
increasing share of post-bleaching cover, matching and then exceeding corymbose *Acropora*
(the most abundant single functional group) by 2023, aligning with recent EcoRRAP
observations (@stbl-9).

Assessing model performance in the post-2017 bleaching years is difficult given the lack of
observations in the years immediately afterwards. The model appears to capture recovery
dynamics well; however, potential mismatches in bleaching mortality and subsequent recovery
may be due to how bleaching is represented (which relies on regional data) and dynamics
specific to localized areas at Moore Reef; an instance of the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem
(as indicated in @sec-results-of-sensitivity-analysis; @fig-2 and @fig-3). Despite this
mismatch, the indicated trends are well aligned with observations falling within ensemble
uncertainty, indicating that the model serves its purpose for indicative projection and
comparative assessment.

![Performance of the ensemble for Moore Reef (n=250). Calibration years spanned
from 1994 to 2016 plus 2021. Available observation years for 2018 and 2020 (LTMP manta tow
for coral cover; post-2017 bleaching event), and 2022 and 2023 (EcoRRAP; to indicate
relative abundance) were used for validation. The first row shows ensemble members
(gray lines) and their mean and best fit (green and blue lines) against manta-tow
observations (dashed light red line with confidence bands). Time points used for model
training/calibration are marked in gold, and the timeframes used for validation highlighted
with a light gray background. The second row illustrates trajectories according to
functional groups with 95% CI. The third row indicates the simulated DHW conditions and
corresponds with observed bleaching events, demonstrating the model responds appropriately
thermal stress. Model performance for both Calibration and Validation periods is indicated in
terms of RMSE and the mean Pearson correlation of log-transformed group cover
($r_{\text{Pearson,log}}$). Note that the years prior to 1994 include a high-disturbance cyclone event (Cyclone Joy, 1990) and so were excluded from model training. Cyclone Yasi also disturbed the reef in 2011; however, the impact on observed cover was comparatively
minor along the reef perimeter.](../figs/16071S_calibration_comparison.png){#fig-6 width="6.001175634295713in" height="4.286554024496938in"}

For Masig Reef, the model exhibits the observed stability in functional group composition
(@stbl-10), perhaps owing to the dominance of large massives in the area. This simplifies
the dynamics and interactions that are required to be represented. Acceptable fit was
achieved during the calibration period, although the ensemble mean slightly overestimates
cover. A similar slight overestimate is seen in the single validation year (ensemble-mean
RMSE of \~0.81%), while the best-performing member closely matches the observation
(\~0.38%). Correlation-based performance metrics are undefined for a single validation
observation and are therefore not reported. The modeled results indicate that smaller reefs
with reduced inter-group dynamics represent a more tractable calibration problem, as
demonstrated here with Masig Reef (full ensemble trajectory detail in @sfig-4).

![Ensemble performance (n=250) for Masig Reef. Calibration years spanned 2021 to
2023, with 2024 reserved for validation (indicated by gray shaded background). The ensemble
tracks the directionality of observed cover with stable trends close to the 2024
observation, with dominance of the large massives evident.](../figs/masig_calibration_comparison.png){#fig-7 width="5.011805555555555in"
height="3.579861111111111in"}

Assessment of factor influence on the composite metric $J$ (@fig-8) revealed that initial
population composition parameters exert the strongest influence on model behavior. At both
reefs, the assumed mean size of large massives was clearly the most influential factor. The
other leading factors were a mix of mean colony sizes and functional-group proportions,
along with colony density at Masig. At Moore, recruitment had comparatively moderate
influence on $J$, similar to colony density and the tabular *Acropora* growth scaler. At
Masig, recruitment and most size-variability (σ) parameters had little influence on $J$
under ensemble-constrained ranges; growth scalers were fixed during calibration at Masig and
so show no influence. Under unconstrained parameter ranges (@sfig-5), the tabular *Acropora*
growth scaler was clearly the most influential factor at Moore, followed by the corymbose
*Acropora* proportion, whereas composition parameters and colony density led at Masig. The
results illustrate the advantage of incorporating available community composition data or
information, as modeled trajectories are heavily influenced by initial states. Naïve
assumptions on composition may lead to unreliable projections, particularly as errors in
functional group dynamics accumulate and compound over time.

![PAWN sensitivity analysis, assessing the influence of parameter values on the
composite metric $J$, with parameter ranges constrained to those identified via ensemble
calibration (n=8,192). Parameters were sampled independently within the ensemble ranges, so
indices describe the region around the ensemble rather than the well-fitting set itself (see
Methods). Factors were sorted by $PAWN_{\text{mean}}$ (highest to lowest; left to
right). Top row shows results for Moore Reef: the assumed mean size of large massives is the
most influential factor, followed by the initialized proportion of large massives and the
size distribution of small massives. Colony density (individuals m^-2^), external
recruitment and self-seeding have comparatively moderate influence. On Masig Reef (bottom
row): the mean size of large massives again leads, followed by colony density, the
large-massive proportion and the mean sizes of tabular *Acropora* and small massives;
recruitment pathways and growth scalers have little
influence.](../figs/sensitivity/combined/combined_constrained_sa.png){#fig-8 width="6.472853237095363in"
height="4.028268810148732in"}

Both recruitment pathways ranked mid-table for the composite metric $J$ at Moore (9th and
11th of 23) and in the lower half at Masig (15th and 17th; @fig-8), and remained broadly
distributed in the calibrated ensemble (Masig range ratios: self-seeding 0.987; external
recruitment 0.985; @fig-9 and @fig-10). Recruitment nonetheless shapes coral cover
trajectories at Moore Reef when its effect is isolated directly (@fig-11). Across the
constrained sample, simulated cover with recruitment rose over the pre-bleaching period
while cover without recruitment declined slowly, so that recruitment-attributable cover grew
to a mean of approximately 19 percentage points by 2016. Following the 2017 bleaching event,
cover recovered by approximately 7.7 percentage points between 2017 and 2023 with
recruitment, compared with 1.1 points without, and recovery was greater with recruitment in
over 99% of samples. The influence of the recruitment pathways on cover also built over time
(@sfig-8). Both were below the dummy threshold in the first simulated years, rose steadily
through the 2000s, and were among the most influential parameters from around 2010 onward.
The mean size of large massives briefly led in the two years after the bleaching event,
before the recruitment pathways again led through to 2023. For recruitment-attributable
cover, the two pathways were the most influential parameters in every year. Absolute cover
in this analysis exceeds that of the calibrated ensemble because the constrained sample does
not reproduce the correlated parameter combinations the ensemble identified (see Methods),
so the contrast between scenarios, rather than cover levels, is of interest.

![Simulated coral cover at Moore Reef across the constrained sample (n = 8,192), with
recruitment as sampled and with both recruitment pathways set to zero. (A) Total coral cover
in each scenario. (B) Recruitment-attributable cover (with minus without recruitment). Lines
show the mean across samples and shaded bands the interquartile range. The dashed red line
marks the 2017 bleaching event. This figure indicates the contrast between
scenarios.](../figs/sensitivity/offshore_north/moore/ensemble/16071S_recruitment_trajectories.png){#fig-11
width="6.5in"}

The ensemble pair plots (Panel A of @fig-9 and @fig-10) show how parameter values vary among
well-fitting model runs. A narrow spread indicates agreement within the ensemble, while a
wide spread means many values remain compatible with the observations. Additional
reef-representative observations of colony density, functional-group composition, and colony
sizes could rule out some of these alternatives, improving parameter identifiability and
reducing uncertainty in the modeled reef state.

Parameter distributions within the ensemble reveal substantial equifinality at both reef
sites (@fig-9 and @fig-10), with most parameters spanning wide ranges across acceptable
parameterizations. Functional-group proportions remain among the least constrained
parameters at both reefs, though the two reefs differ in character. At Moore Reef, the
proportions are comparatively uniform and loosely constrained (all range ratios above 0.5),
whereas at Masig they span a wider spread, ranging from a comparatively well-constrained
large-massive proportion (0.303) to a nearly unconstrained corymbose *Acropora* proportion
(0.913). Growth scalers are a predictable exception at both sites, as these are
location-specific forcing factors intended to represent local conditions. At Masig, the five
mean-size parameters occupy a narrower, more consistent band than the proportions (range
ratios 0.393 -- 0.751 versus 0.303 -- 0.913), consistent with the relatively higher
sensitivity of mean colony size to cover trajectories at that reef; the single most tightly
constrained proportion is nonetheless narrower than any mean-size parameter. Further
assessment of parameter interactions is provided in Supplementary E. Range ratios summarize
each calibrated parameter's spread as $(\max - \min)/(\max + \min)$; Panel B of @fig-9 and
@fig-10 instead compares the standard deviations of the calibration-bounds prior and
calibrated ensemble, so the two measures are not required to align.

Note that the PAWN influence and the reduction in parameter spread across the calibrated
ensemble do not need to align. At Moore Reef, calibration reduced the standard deviation of
the three most influential factors relative to the calibration-bounds prior by 41.4% for the
mean size of large massives, 25.0% for the proportion of large massives, and 24.6% for the
mean size of small massives (@fig-9, Panel B). At Masig Reef, calibration reduced the
standard deviation by 30.1% for the mean size of large massives and 31.6% for colony
density, but by only 5.6% for the large-massive proportion, whose bounds were already
informed by EcoRRAP observations (@tbl-4; @fig-10, Panel B). At Masig, mean large-massive
size and colony density also trade off strongly (r = −0.817; @fig-10, Panel A), so observed
cover can be reproduced by fewer, larger colonies or by more, smaller ones. The
large-massive proportion is reduced least, consistent with its strong trade-off against the
small-massive proportion (r = −0.736; @stbl-8). Because group proportions are
interdependent, constraining the share of one or more functional groups (e.g., through
additional monitoring data) also constrains the others.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

A fundamental challenge in ecological modeling is constraining complexity while retaining
sufficient fidelity with respect to its purpose. Kora balances ecological realism with
computational efficiency by narrowing the represented mechanisms to maintain parsimony with
respect to available data. Coral colony diameter and functional group were selected as key
structural elements to represent in the model through sensitivity analysis of available
data.

Unnecessarily increasing complexity introduces pitfalls that are now extensively documented
in broader modeling literature [@christieSimplicityComplexityModelling2011;
@jakemanNormalizingGoodPractice2024; @majonePitfallsAnalysis1980;
@razaviFutureSensitivityAnalysis2021; @voinovIntegronstersIntegralIntegrated2013]. These
include reduced parameter identifiability, decreased interpretability, and increases to data
requirements and computational burden [@croutMyModelToo2009;
@guillaumeIntroductoryOverviewIdentifiability2019;
@iwanagaSociotechnicalScalesSocioenvironmental2021;
@luoParameterIdentifiabilityConstraint2009]. When data are insufficient to validate
additional structures, validation defaults to expert opinion, potentially introducing
modeler bias if not elicited and applied with care [@drescherRigorousUseExpert2013;
@glynnDataDecisionsProcessing2017].

Kora's development demonstrates an alternative workflow leveraging newly collected
large-area 3D photogrammetry data from the EcoRRAP monitoring program. Model specification
was guided by PAWN sensitivity analysis of empirical observations, which identified colony
diameter as the dominant proxy for demographic rates across functional groups
(@sec-model-development-workflow). The resulting regressions coupled with representation of
exogenous disturbances demonstrated acceptable skill in reproducing past observations,
increasing confidence in modeled projections under future conditions despite irreducible
uncertainty in future DHW trends and ecological dynamics. Recent research has also shown
that colony size plays a major role in the impact of heat stress on bleaching severity
[@alvarez-noriegaChallengingParadigmsRole2025] and legacy effect on vital rates
[@lecheneLegacyEffectsMild2026] of corals in the GBR.

Constituent regression performance varied by process and functional group. Held-out
size-binned survival fits differed among groups (@sec-survival-models). Tabular *Acropora*
showed moderate linear agreement (Pearson 0.60) but almost no rank-order agreement
(Kendall's τ 0.001); branching non-*Acropora* showed stronger linear agreement (0.76) but
more limited rank-order agreement (0.43), while corymbose *Acropora* retained relatively
strong rank-order agreement (0.73). The calibrated ensembles nevertheless reproduced
reef-level cover trajectories at both demonstration reefs (@sec-results), so constituent and
population-level fit should be assessed separately.

The finding that initial colony diameter and functional group represent demographic
variation provides an empirical basis for adopting this model structure elsewhere, even
where local conditions differ. Though this should not be taken to mean that parameter values
or relative importance will be consistent between contexts. Certainly, the three to four
years of EcoRRAP data provide a limited window of information and may not capture the
potential range of vital rates and environmental disturbance. PAWN was selected for its ease
of use and communication, though practitioners adopting this workflow are encouraged to
complement it with additional sensitivity analysis methods given the diversity of available
approaches [@douglas-smithCertainTrendsUncertainty2020;
@pianosiSensitivityAnalysisEnvironmental2016a; @saltelliGlobalSensitivityAnalysis2007;
@wangPracticalExperienceSensitivity2019].

The ensemble calibration approach makes uncertainty an explicit structured output. Rather
than conditioning on a single parameter set, the ensemble represents the full range of
parameter combinations consistent with observed reef states [akin to Pattern-Oriented
Modelling approaches; @grimmPatternorientedModellingPopulation1996], allowing the
calibration to reveal where the model is and is not identifiable from available data.
Furthermore, the approach reframes equifinality from a modeling liability into
decision-relevant information. The approach makes the structure of the uncertainty explicit,
identifying where and what additional data would most improve projection skill relative to
initial assumptions (the priors). Parameters that remain non-identifiable after calibration
indicate genuine data limitations rather than model failure and point directly to monitoring
priorities. Sensitivity is not identifiability: at Masig, the influential large- and
small-massive proportions trade off, and group-resolved cover observations could help
distinguish them.

## Ecological findings and monitoring implications

A consistent finding across both demonstration reefs is that initial population composition
and relative abundance were more influential on calibration fitness than process parameters
under observed DHW conditions. Constraining the initial (or current) community state may
therefore be a priority for short-horizon projections, although its forecast benefit
relative to refining vital rates was not tested. Configuring Kora to represent corals by
broad functional groups defined by their morphological and demographic characteristics, and
their sensitivity to disturbance (e.g., fast, intermediate, or slow growing; competitive vs
stress-tolerant) rather than their specific taxa or species may be sufficient depending on
model purpose. This simplification, however, does not resolve the question of where a single
parameterization remains valid.

This composition sensitivity is not uniform across functional groups or reefs. The mean size
of large massives is clearly the leading parameter at both reefs, but the other leading
composition parameters differ. At Moore they include the large-massive proportion and the
small-massive size distribution, whereas at Masig colony density and the large-massive
proportion follow (@fig-8). These influential parameters remain only loosely constrained by
the available data (@fig-9 and @fig-10), so reef-representative observations of
functional-group composition and colony size structure would most directly reduce the
remaining uncertainty.

The GBR is well-documented as a network of ecologically distinct ecosystems
[@alvarez-noriegaSpatialVariationUpper2024; @jurriaansWaveEnergyOther2025;
@whitmanSeededAcroporaDigitifera2025]. Applying the same model parameterization and
configuration across multiple locations therefore requires assessing transferability
[@radchukTransferabilityMechanisticEcological2019;
@wengerAssessingTransferabilityEcological2012] or performing location-specific
(re-)calibration, depending on the intended purpose [@jakemanTenIterativeSteps2006;
@jakemanNormalizingGoodPractice2024]. Which of these is warranted depends on the spatial
resolution and required accuracy or precision for the decision support task. A single
generalized parameterization may perform sufficiently well for broad indicative regional
guidance. For site-specific decisions, assessing transferability and recalibrating would
require repeated local diameter and survival observations across sites, depths and thermal
conditions, paired with environmental and functional-group monitoring.

In cases where such high spatial detail is necessary, parameter correlation analysis
indicates that ensemble uncertainty is structurally organized. The proportion-size trade-off
within functional groups (@sec-results) means models can agree on total coral cover while
disagreeing on its composition - which coral types are present and in what proportions
(@stbl-7 and @stbl-8). The use of EcoRRAP data constrained modelled community state, under
the assumption that the available data is representative of the reef. Further data speaking
to the relative abundance of each functional group would help reduce this structural
uncertainty.

The two recruitment pathways (externally sourced larvae and self-seeding) are a partial
exception to this framing. Both are among the least identifiable parameters in the ensemble
(@sec-results), yet recruitment as a whole drives much of the simulated recovery at Moore
Reef. Isolating its contribution shows that recruitment sustains cover through the
pre-bleaching period and accounts for most of the post-bleaching recovery, with its
influence on cover building over decades rather than being confined to a short window after
disturbance (@fig-11 and @sfig-8). The two pathways are poorly identified individually
because they compensate for one another in the calibrated ensemble ($r$ = −0.82; @stbl-7),
so their combined contribution is better constrained than either alone. This mirrors
patterns identified elsewhere. Recovery after disturbances in remote reefs only begin once
juveniles have reached maturity, indicating a reliance on self-recruitment
[@gilmourRecoveryIsolatedCoral2013], and the abundance of juvenile corals has been found to
be an indicator that a reef is more likely to recover than undergo a regime shift to
macroalgal dominance [@grahamPredictingClimatedrivenRegime2015].

The influence of recruitment on the calibration objective is nonetheless only moderate, as
the composite objective averages over the full multi-decade calibration period and the two
pathways trade off against each other. The apparent unidentifiability of the recruitment
parameters may therefore reflect the time-averaged formulation of the objective, and the
lack of data that would separate the two pathways, rather than a lack of influence. This
suggests two complementary monitoring and modeling priorities specific to recruitment.
First, targeted recruit density surveys conducted one to three years after a disturbance
event [cf. @stratfordFatetrackingEarlyCoral2025] to constrain uncertainty in estimates of
juvenile abundance (for the purpose of modelling projections), and second, objective
functions that directly consider recruitment-sensitive periods, and the role settlers and
juveniles play in post-disturbance recovery. If the modeling is to obtain indicative
regional projections, then use of data pooled from multiple sources is potentially feasible
[cf. @chaseDisentanglingImportanceEcological2011; @evansSimpleModelsLead2013;
@coelhoParsimoniousViewParsimony2019]. At this spatial scale, the recruitment *pathway* may
matter less than total recruitment magnitude for reproducing cover trajectories, with
post-recruitment mortality further diminishing the effect of recruitment source [cf.
@evansEarlyRecoveryDynamics2020]. Depending on the modeling context, purpose, and
timeframes, recruitment pathways may therefore be lumped to further simplify the model.
Otherwise, constraining uncertainty in recruitment pathways may ultimately require
hydrodynamic and larval connectivity modeling validated against costly genetic analyses,
especially if the intended aim is site-specific management or conservation planning.

Kora's data requirements for application are kept deliberately minimal. Kora can begin
ensemble calibration with coral-cover observations alone; functional-group composition and
other observations can then be incorporated to constrain plausible states. The Moore and
Masig results use this data-enriched stage and do not measure the improvement over a
cover-only baseline. Where empirical observations are unavailable, expert-elicited estimates
of growth, survival, size frequency distributions, or cover trajectories could provide a
sufficient basis for exploratory assessment. Although the extent to which such
expert-elicited information can substitute for empirical observations remains uncertain, it
provides a starting point for model development and hypothesis generation.

## Current limitations and future opportunities

An intended future application is to characterize the implications of conservation and
management activities where corals are seeded or transplanted. Efforts were focused on
identifying and representing coral dynamics at the targeted spatial scale. As a result, only
heat-related disturbances are currently represented, as bleaching is the prime concern for
climate change projections. Incorporating additional acute stressors such as cyclone strikes
or wave-driven damage requires further research into their demographic impacts before
informed representation is possible [cf. @dixonCoralReefExposure2022;
@whitmanSeededAcroporaDigitifera2025].

Location-specific growth scaling terms absorb the influence of local nutrient levels,
predation, and other chronic stressors. They act as a lumped proxy for influences that
cannot be individually resolved with the available data. At Moore Reef, a controlled
diagnostic that fixed the tabular and corymbose *Acropora* growth scalers to 1.0 (rather
than allowing the calibrated range) degraded calibration fitness by about a sixth. Despite
the underlying colony-level growth regressions themselves being well fit ($R^2 \geq 0.9$),
the fitness threshold was not reached in any trial. This is not to imply that the
regressions are incorrect or poorly specified, rather they indicate that additional factors
at the reef-scale, annualized simulation level are influencing growth outcomes.

As discussed above, however, these influences remain unidentifiable from single time-point
composition data; longitudinal surveys capturing temporal cover change would be required to
constrain them, and further diagnostic work would be needed to determine whether the
specific corrections at Moore Reef -- a ~67% downward adjustment for tabular *Acropora*
(posterior mean ≈0.33) and a ~52% upward adjustment for corymbose *Acropora* (posterior mean
≈1.52) -- reflect annualization/interval bias in the fitted growth curves, the
space-constraint interaction, or another structural source. An accompanying scaling term for
coral survival could also be considered, though at the cost of additional complexity and
parameter interactions. Both terms are currently treated as fixed constants within a fixed
model structure, which assumes homoskedasticity. It may be desirable in future to expand
this parameterization to represent coral reefs in a more spatially explicit manner suited to
the needs of a given modeling exercise.

The depth amelioration relationship follows @bairdDeclineBleachingSuggests2018, in which
bleaching severity decreases monotonically with depth. This is well-supported for the
clear-water offshore sites demonstrated here, although
@alvarez-noriegaChallengingParadigmsRole2025 document that this pattern can reverse in
turbid inshore environments, where deeper reef areas may experience equal or greater thermal
stress. Transferability to reef environments with substantially different physical regimes
warrants further analysis and validation.

The EcoRRAP monitoring design excludes colonies larger than 2 m diameter from continuous
observation, biasing the model towards small to medium colonies; regressions are capped to
the largest observed sizes to avoid extrapolation beyond the range of the training data.
Transects were configured to an assumed 9 m depth, though the general practical range for
monitoring and conservation efforts is typically up to 15 m [cf.
@howlettActiveCoralPropagation2023]. There is evidence that deeper reef areas may provide
thermal refugia [@bairdDeclineBleachingSuggests2018; @grierImportanceDepthRefugia2026;
@sunClimateRefugiaGreat2024] and excluding them may give a misleading view of
population-level decline. Similarly, Kora does not account for many factors that may
influence coral population dynamics. These are many and include interaction effects between
coral species, competition with macroalgae [cf. @baskettResponseDiversityCan2014], predation
pressure (such as fish or invertebrate grazers including Crown-of-Thorns seastars), or
temporal variability in available coral habitat, as influenced by, for example, the
formation and stabilization of rubble fields [@liuAcceleratingCoralRubble2024a].

The breeder's equation approach to estimate adaptation represents key adaptive dynamics
without explicit genetic simulation. It is a simplified representation which necessarily
omits complexities such as genetic architecture, correlations between tolerance and other
traits, and detailed population genetic dynamics [@morrisseyDangerApplyingBreeders2010]. For
management questions focused on short timescales of years rather than generations, however,
this trade-off between model simplicity and biological realism seems justified.

Several avenues exist to extend Kora's current single-location architecture. A
component-based model architecture [cf. @iwanagaSociotechnicalScalesSocioenvironmental2021;
@littleTieredSystemofsystemsModeling2019; @valeTwentyeightYearsComponentbased2016] would
enable more flexible, location-specific system compositions, allowing a network of
representative reef areas to be constructed and interconnected. Computational cost would
likely increase without changes to how colony diameters are tracked [cf.
@ribeirodealmeidaCoralBloxComputationallyEfficient2026] or further simplification of model
structure.

The demonstrated value of single-model ensemble calibration also motivates exploration of
multi-model ensemble approaches, where projections are drawn from structurally distinct
models rather than parameter variants of one. In hydrology and ecosystem service modeling,
multi-model ensembles consistently reduce systematic bias and improve projection
reliability, with ensemble means or weighted combinations typically outperforming any
individual model [@abramowitzESDReviewsModel2019; @arsenaultComparativeAnalysis92015;
@wangComparisonHydrologicalModel2021a; @willcockEnsemblesEcosystemService2020a].

While assembling sufficiently independent model ensembles presents a practical challenge
given the limited availability of openly accessible coral reef models, the potential gains
in projection reliability make this a worthwhile direction. CoralPOP
[@browneCoralPOPMorphologybasedCoral2026], a functional-based, size-structured population
model independently validated across the GBR and Caribbean, represents one such candidate,
alongside Kora, for inclusion in a future multi-model ensemble. Entity Component Systems
coupled with Physics-informed or Scientific Machine Learning represent a complementary path
toward spatially explicit, computationally efficient representations at GBR scale
[@langeArkecsArkjlArkjl2025; @redmondExploringTheoryPractice2025], enabling further
incorporation of acute disturbances and potentially non-stationary system processes.
Temporally, gap-filling methods, such as those explored in
@vercelloniPredictingCoralCover2025, may assist further constraining the uncertainties
involved.

More broadly, modeling for decision support in the GBR and elsewhere remains hindered by
limited investment in open science practices. While numerous models have been published, few
are openly available with accompanying source code and user documentation, and fewer still
accept external contributions. This leads to a perceived lack of transparency and
accessibility that complicates independent assessment of model suitability for a given
purpose. Issues of reproducibility and researcher dependency further limit the field's
capacity to advance; models in continual use are typically developed and maintained by a
small number of researchers, and longevity is compromised as those who initiated development
retire [@addorLegacyRatherAdequacy2019; @baker1500ScientistsLift2016;
@bomzonScholarlyPublishingScientific2021; @hutCommentMostComputational2017;
@huttonMostComputationalHydrology2016; @michelettiGuidesProtocolsAcronyms2024]. The
situation is beginning to change, with recent open, size- or morphology-structured models
such as CoralBlox [@ribeirodealmeidaCoralBloxComputationallyEfficient2026] and CoralPOP
[@browneCoralPOPMorphologybasedCoral2026] published with accompanying source code. Kora and
the analyses presented here are similarly open-source and open-access. Transitioning the
broader modeling community toward open, modular frameworks [cf.
@holzworthAPSIMNextGeneration2018; @knobenModularAssessmentRainfall2019;
@molinSuperflexPy120Open2020] that embrace these principles is essential for coral reef
modeling science to progress at the pace required by management challenges under future
uncertainty.

A key strength of the workflow presented here is that model design is directly informed by
empirical data and can be updated as more comprehensive observations become available.
Additional years of vital rate measurements, empirical characterization of local
environmental conditions (water flow, structural complexity, light regime), expanded colony
size ranges, and incorporation of additional taxa each represent concrete pathways through
which the sensitivity-guided workflow could be revisited and uncertainty in projectiosn
systematically reduced.

# Conclusion

Empirical sensitivity analysis of Great Barrier Reef coral demographic data identified
colony diameter and functional group as the most consistent influences on growth and
survival, while location-specific factors played a greater role in survival at the more
environmentally heterogeneous Offshore North sites. These findings grounded the structure of
Kora on the basis of available data and excluded factors whose effects could not be
distinguished from random variation. The approach tempers reliance on factors whose
inclusion would otherwise be primarily motivated by ecological plausibility or literature.

The resulting model is highly efficient, with sub-second simulation times that enable
extensive ensemble exploration while remaining practical for stakeholder engagement and
interactive decision-making. Ensemble calibration at Moore Reef and Masig Reef demonstrated
that Kora can reproduce observed coral cover trajectories while maintaining plausible
population compositions. The resulting equifinality was structured, with multiple
demographic configurations capable of generating outcomes consistent with available
observations. This makes the ensemble particularly valuable under deep uncertainty: rather
than requiring extensive data to resolve uncertainty before projections can be made, it
explicitly characterizes the range of community compositions and demographic dynamics
supported by the available evidence. The presented framework remains applicable in cases
where monitoring is limited to periodic coral cover estimates.

Although sensitivity-guided model development and ensemble calibration are well established
in fields such as hydrology and terrestrial ecosystem modeling, their systematic application
to marine ecological projections remains uncommon. The core contribution is therefore a
transferable workflow for sensitivity-guided model development and ensemble-based
uncertainty characterization, providing a practical means of generating uncertainty-aware
projections from achievable monitoring and supporting timely, model-informed reef management
under accelerating environmental change.

# Supplementary A: Software Implementation Details {#sec-supplementary-a .unnumbered}

Kora is implemented in Julia (v1.12) and is available at
<https://github.com/open-AIMS/Kora.jl>. The analysis scripts accompanying this study are
available at: <https://github.com/ConnectedSystems/Kora_2025-11-01_study>.

**Performance characteristics**

Estimates for a standard desktop workstation:

+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Configuration                                                      | Runtime             |
+:===================================================================+:====================+
| Single simulation, 1 location, 10-year horizon                     | \~0.01 seconds      |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Single simulation, 1 location, 75-year horizon                     | \~0.35 seconds      |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Calibrated ensemble, 250 candidates, 1 location, 75-year horizon   | \~10 seconds        |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------------+

**Reproducibility**

All results presented in this study can be reproduced by running the numbered analysis
scripts (00a--05) in the accompanying repository in sequence. Serialized intermediate
outputs are cached to disk to avoid redundant computation on re-runs. Random seeds are fixed
throughout.

**License**

Kora.jl is released under the MIT license.

**Environmental data depth assignment**

Environmental variables from eReefs are available across discrete depth levels. For
temperature assignment, observations at 9 m below the surface were designated as the target
depth. When data at this exact depth was unavailable for a given plot-date combination, a
hierarchical depth-matching procedure was applied: (1) use exact target depth (−9.0 m) if
available, and (2) if not available, use the nearest shallower depth. The collation code
also permits records without a specified depth as a last resort, but none were selected in
this extraction. This approach balances fidelity to the intended sampling depth with
maximizing spatial-temporal coverage of environmental covariates. The procedure was applied
transparently with diagnostic reporting quantifying coverage gaps and recording which
fallback depths were substituted, allowing assessment of potential bias introduced by
depth-based assignment.

## Computational Scalability {.unnumbered}

Understanding how the model scales computationally is essential for planning model
application across different spatial contexts as they affect the resources required. For a
single represented area and five functional groups, Kora involves 58 factors, although not
all are required to be considered for a given application. Here, Big O notation is used to
indicate the upper bound of model scalability with respect to its dimensionality (the number
of parameters). @stbl-1 outlines a breakdown of the parameter count by model component.

Model dimensionality is expected to scale linearly with the number of locations or
functional groups individually: either $O\left( N_{l} \right)$ or $O(N_{f})$, where $N_{(
\cdot )}$ denotes the total number of locations ($l$) or groups ($f$). If both dimensions
increase simultaneously, however, the parameter space scales bilinearly as $O(N_{l} \cdot
N_{f})$ due to group-location interaction. In practice, however, the consequent explosion in
parametric uncertainty is constrained as application of Kora is typically focused on a
single representative area.

Recent analyses suggest that 5 to 10 functional groups may be sufficient to represent
diverse reef functions [see analyses in @mcwilliamCapturingDimensionsCoral2026]. If adopted,
this limits $N_{f} \leq 10$ such that the dimensional scaling is effectively linear with the
number of locations for the intended model purpose. Alternatively, if obtaining an
indication of coral cover alone is the objective, then this could potentially be achieved by
a single coral group representing the "average" coral, and $N_{f}$ would be fixed to 1. That
said, the utility of such an indication would be very focused to a specific purpose
dependent solely on coral cover.

Increasing represented area is expected to scale at or near $O(n)$ , assuming all else
remains the same, as an increase in area is likely to increase the number of individuals
required to be tracked. A related consideration is that very large areas or numbers of
"representative areas" could potentially exhaust available memory. Potential approaches to
mitigate this limitation, as well as introducing more spatially explicit representation of
reef habitat are found in the Discussion (@sec-discussion).

+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

+==================================+=======================================================================================================================+
| $$X_{t}$$                        | Set of diameters (in cm) representing a population of coral at time $t$                                               |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$d_{i,t}$$                      | Coral diameter at time $t$ (cm), where $d_{i,t} \subset X_{t}$                                                        |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$f$$                            | Functional group                                                                                                      |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$l$$                            | Location index (examples only consider a single location)                                                             |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$f_{g}$$                        | Growth function for functional group $f$                                                                              |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$f_{s}$$                        | Survival function for functional group $f$                                                                            |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$C_{t}$$                        | Coral cover at time $t$ (m²)                                                                                          |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$K$$                            | Global carrying capacity (m²); maximum coral habitable area (see $K_{l}$ for location-specific)                       |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\theta$$                       | Degree heating weeks (DHW)                                                                                            |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\mu_{\theta_{\text{tol}}}$$    | Mean thermal tolerance (DHW)                                                                                          |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\sigma_{\theta_{\text{tol}}}$$ | Standard deviation of DHW tolerance                                                                                   |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\delta$$                       | Depth (m)                                                                                                             |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$h²$$                           | Narrow-sense heritability                                                                                             |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$L$$                            | Larval production                                                                                                     |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$G_{t}()$$                      | Population-level growth operator                                                                                      |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$g_{t}(d)$$                     | Individual-level growth function (diameter $d$ at time $t$)                                                           |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$S()$$                          | Survival probability                                                                                                  |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$M$$                            | Mortality rate                                                                                                        |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\alpha$$                       | Scaling coefficient                                                                                                   |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$A_{l}$$                        | Available coral habitable space                                                                                       |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$D_{\max}$$                     | Maximum settler density                                                                                               |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$L_{l,f}$$                      | Larvae seeking settlement (for location *l*, group $f$)                                                               |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$K_{l}$$                        | Total/Maximum coral habitable space for location $l$                                                                  |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$Z_{t}$$                        | Population of survivors after background mortality at time $t$                                                        |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\theta_{\text{eff}}$$          | Effective thermal stress (depth-adjusted DHW)                                                                         |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$P_{\text{affected}}$$          | Proportion of population affected by bleaching                                                                        |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$d_{0}$$                        | Colony size threshold for thermal resistance (150 cm)                                                                 |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\alpha_{\text{depth}}$$        | Depth coefficient ameliorating heat stress                                                                            |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$y$$                            | Observed values in calibration dataset                                                                                |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\widehat{y}$$                  | Modeled/predicted values                                                                                              |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\tilde{r}$$                    | Correlation loss component ($1 - r$)                                                                                  |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$v$$                            | Variability ratio (modeled vs. observed)                                                                              |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$B$$                            | Bias ratio (mean modeled vs. mean observed)                                                                           |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\alpha$$                       | Variability loss component ($1 - v$) (distinct from scaling coefficient)                                              |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$L_B$$                          | Bias loss component ($1 - B$) (distinct from polynomial coefficient)                                                  |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$T_{E}$$                        | Number of EcoRRAP observation timesteps                                                                               |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$N$$                            | Last year in observation period                                                                                       |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                  | **Performance measures**                                                                                              |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$KGE$$ / $$NKGE$$               | Kling-Gupta Efficiency score and Normalized Kling-Gupta Efficiency score                                              |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$RMSE$$                         | Root Mean Square Error                                                                                                |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$r$$                            | Pearson correlation coefficient                                                                                       |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\rho_{\log}$$                  | Log-correlation loss: $1 - r(\log(\widehat{x_{f}}), \log(x_{f}))$ (training objective)                                |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$r_{\text{Pearson,log}}$$       | Pearson correlation between log-transformed functional group cover (reporting metric)                                 |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$W_{E}$$                        | Additional penalty placed on extrema of observations based on absolute error used for model training/fitting (i.e.,   |
|                                  | first and last observations)                                                                                          |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$\phi_{f}$$                     | Penalty term adding the number of functional groups which had zero contribution to total cover for three or more      |
|                                  | timesteps. It is assumed that local extinction is an implausible occurrence under historic conditions.                |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$z_{f}$$                        | Cover trajectory ($z$) for a given functional group $f$.                                                              |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $$J()$$                          | Composite metric used for calibration:                                                                                |
|                                  | $$J\left( y,\widehat{y} \right) = (\tilde{r} + \alpha + L_B) + W_{E} + \phi_{f}\left( x_{f} \right) + \rho_{\log}$$   |
+----------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

# Supplementary D: Adaptive Quantile Binning method {#supplementary-d-adaptive-quantile-binning-method .unnumbered}

The adaptive minimum sample binning algorithm partitions a dataset into bins ($b$) while
ensuring each bin contains at least a specified minimum number of samples ($m$). Code to
perform the partitioning described below is provided in the Kora.jl package.

Given a dataset with $n$ observations:

$$\text{x} = \{ x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\ldots,x_{n}\}$$

The maximum number of bins $b$ that can be created while satisfying the minimum constraint
is:

$$b = \lfloor\frac{n}{m}\rfloor$$

noting that $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor$ denotes integer division here. The target bin size
$s_{target}$ and remainder $r$ are computed as:

$$s_{target} = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{b} \right\rfloor,\ r = n\ mod\ b$$

Where $mod$ denotes the modulo operation. Here, it is required that $s_{target} \geq m$.

Samples are then distributed across bins by sorting $\mathbf{x}$ in ascending order. The
permutation is indicated with $\pi$, such that
$x_{\pi(1)} \leq x_{\pi(2)} \leq \ldots \leq x_{\pi(n)}$. The size of the $i$-th bin is
defined as:

$$s_{i} = \left\{ \begin{aligned}
s_{target} + 1\ \  & if\ i \leq r \\
s_{target}\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \  & if\ i > r
\end{aligned} \right.\ $$

ensuring that $\sum_{i = 1}^{b}{s_{i} = n}$ and the remainder are distributed evenly across
the first $r$ bins.

Cumulative bin bounds are $c_{0} = 0$ and
$c_{i} = \sum_{j = 1}^{i}s_{j}for\ i = 1,\ldots,b$. The bin assignment function
$\beta:\left\{ 1,\ldots,n \right\} \rightarrow \{ 1,\ldots,b\}$ maps each observation to its
bin:

$$\beta(k) = i,\ c_{i - 1} < \pi^{- 1}(k) \leq c_{i}$$

Where $\pi^{- 1}(k)$ denotes the rank of observation $k$ in the sorted order. Observation
$x_{k}$ is assigned to bin $i$ if its sorted position falls within the range allocated to
that bin.

The binning approach guarantees each bin contains at least $m$ samples, the number of
observations in each bin is balanced, differing by at most 1 and the natural ordering of
observations are preserved as the partitioning is applied sequentially on sorted data.

## Parameter Interactions {.unnumbered}

Assessment of parameter interactions identifies compensatory relationships with $|r|$ \>
0.5 for seven parameter pairs at each reef (@stbl-7, @stbl-8, @sfig-6 and @sfig-7). At Moore
Reef, the strongest correlations are a mean--standard-deviation trade-off for tabular
*Acropora* colony sizes ($r$ = −0.823) and a trade-off between the two recruitment pathways
($r$ = −0.823). Because external recruitment and self-seeding compensate for one another,
calibration constrains their combined contribution more than either pathway individually.
Within-group proportion--size trade-offs are present for small massives (proportion--mean,
$r$ = −0.676), large massives (proportion--standard deviation, $r$ = −0.676) and branching
non-*Acropora* (proportion--mean, $r$ = −0.588). The tabular *Acropora* growth scaler is
positively correlated with tabular *Acropora* size variability ($r$ = 0.528) and with the
mean size of corymbose *Acropora* ($r$ = 0.523), indicating that the growth correction
partly compensates for the initial size structure. At Masig Reef, the dominant pattern
instead reflects the tightly-bounded, large-massive-dominated group composition (see
Methods): colony density trades off against the mean size of large massives ($r$ = −0.817),
and cross-group proportion trade-offs against the large-massive group are present for small
massive ($r$ = −0.736), branching non-*Acropora* ($r$ = −0.638) and corymbose *Acropora*
($r$ = −0.591) proportions. A proportion--mean-size trade-off persists for corymbose
*Acropora* ($r$ = −0.572), alongside a mean--standard-deviation trade-off for tabular
*Acropora* ($r$ = −0.663). The recruitment trade-off is also present at Masig ($r$ =
−0.554), indicating this compensatory relationship is not specific to either site's data
availability. The correlation structure at Moore Reef predominantly reflects within-group
size-distribution and proportion--size trade-offs together with the recruitment trade-off,
whereas at Masig Reef it remains dominated by cross-group proportion trade-offs against the
large massive group and density's coupling to that group's mean size — consistent with
Masig's proportion bounds being tightened around the reef's strongly large-massive-dominated
observed composition.

## EcoRRAP-derived functional group cover {.unnumbered}

@stbl-11 lists the EcoRRAP benthic labelset classes used to estimate functional group cover
and the functional group each was assigned to (@sec-functional-groups). Classes without an
assigned functional group were excluded.

::: {#stbl-11}
: Mapping of EcoRRAP benthic labelset classes to Kora functional groups for the cover estimates.

| Code | Benthic class | Functional group |
|---|---|---|
| ACX | Acropora Bottlebrush | tabular *Acropora* |
| ACT | Acropora table | tabular *Acropora* |
| AC_Bran_OTH | Acropora Branching Other | corymbose *Acropora* |
| ACO_OTH | Acropora corymbose other | corymbose *Acropora* |
| ACD | Acropora digitate | corymbose *Acropora* |
| S_POC_ACU | Pocillopora acuta | branching non-*Acropora* |
| S_POC_DAM | Pocillopora damicornis | branching non-*Acropora* |
| G_POC_OTH | Pocillopora other | branching non-*Acropora* |
| S_POC_VER | Pocillopora verrucosa | branching non-*Acropora* |
| G_SER | Seriatopora hystrix | branching non-*Acropora* |
| G_STY | Stylophora pistillata | branching non-*Acropora* |
| CB_OTH_ARB | other Branching Non-acropora Arborescent | branching non-*Acropora* |
| CB_OTH_C | other Branching Non-acropora Coarse | branching non-*Acropora* |
| CB_OTH_F | other Branching Non-acropora fine | branching non-*Acropora* |
| G_AST | Astreopora | Small massives |
| G_DIP | Diploastrea | Small massives |
| MAS_FL | Flower-like Massive | Small massives |
| G_GOS | Goniastrea | Small massives |
| G_LEP | Leptoria | Small massives |
| MAS_OTH | Massive other | Small massives |
| G_PLA | Platygyra | Small massives |
| G_POR | Porites massive | Large massives |
:::

Functional group cover (@stbl-9, @stbl-10) was estimated by summing, per transect, the cover
of all benthic classes assigned to a given functional group (@stbl-11). These were then
averaged for all transects within a reef surveyed for each year. Where a class had no
recorded value for a transect, it was omitted from that transect's sum. No additional
uncertainty propagation (e.g., across transects or classes) was applied for the purpose of
the modelling/analysis.
